📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when Newly introduced York City mayor Zohran Mamdani passed out water bottles to marathoners on Nov. 1, few clocked the newly mustachioned man as the city’s head honcho. After all, he’s the first bearded NYC mayor in over a century after, and his constituents had grown familiar with his signature look. When images of his new facial hair circulated, people wondered what inspired the change. Had the mayor been influenced by his hip Brooklyn constituents enough to grow his own on-trend mustache? As we learned the day after the marathon in an online video, the mustache was in support of a somewhat-ancient tradition: Movember.

If it feels like no one’s talked about Movember for a while, that’s because the non-profit charity’s heyday online peaked in 2012. That year, according to the Australian-based foundation, over 1.1 million people participated in Movember—a campaign that encourages men to grow mustaches to raise awareness and funds for men’s mental health, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer—collecting more than $126 million in charity. But like planking, “Gangnam Style,” and flash mobs, Movember eventually faded from the cultural conversation. Google Trends recorded a 10% drop in searches for the cause the following year, and by 2026, search interest had fallen 90% from its 2012 peak. Now, after Mamdani, alongside Council Member Rita Joseph, unveiled a $4 million investment in a newly introduced prostate cancer center at Brooklyn’s Kings County Hospital in honor of the hairy month-long social movement, interest in Movember has since climbed to its highest level since 2019, according to Google Trends.

While the mayor’s stubble has come and gone throughout the month, the heavy mustache has remained constant.

In a recent development, the stubble around the mustache has come and gone during the month, but that thick mustache has remained a staple. He had it at a Veterans Day reception, during a plethora of press conferences, and when he declared the disbanding of the New York Police Department’s controversial Strategic Response Group.

Politicians have long been defined, at least in part, by their hair: Donald Trump’s comb-over, Bernie Sanders’ horseshoe-shaped hairline, Gavin Newsom’s slicked-back locks. But facial hair is increasingly becoming part of the political image, too, as more men embrace letting their beards grow. Pete Buttigieg, once clean-shaven, grew a beard after leaving his post as Transportation Secretary; JD Vance became the first bearded vice president in decades; and Mamdani ended more than a century’s worth of clean-shaven NYC mayors.

And hey, what better time to revive an early 2010s tradition than following the Democrats’ historic victories in the midterm elections. Millennial woke optimism is back, baby, and so is growing facial hair for a charitable cause. If the mayor’s facial hair can turn a bygone internet fad into renewed attention for men’s health, it may be his most consequential grooming decision yet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With busy schedules and limited time each day, slow cookers are key to getting dinner on the table. They can take simple ingredients and transform them into a complete, ready-to-eat meal. Because the slow cooker does all the work for you, you may think that it can also handle defrosting meat.

In a recent development, but think again. The idea seems convenient in theory, but in practice, it raises some serious food safety concerns. We consulted health experts to learn more about adding frozen meat to a slow cooker. So next time you plan a hands-off dinner, you can make sure your food is delicious and safe to eat.

Sorry to be the bearer of bad news: You should never put frozen meat directly into your slow cooker. “I am all for cutting out unnecessary steps in cooking, but using frozen meat in your slow cooker is not one of them,” states Melissa Koch, RD, MEd.

Raw meat can carry harmful bacteria that cause foodborne illness. Freezing stops them from multiplying, but doesn't necessarily kill them. And because slow cookers heat food gradually, frozen meat can spend too long in what food safety experts call the “temperature danger zone.”.

“The danger zone refers to a temperature range of 40°F (4°C) to 140°F (60°C) over two or more hours when harmful bacteria grow or multiply at a fast rate,” Koch explains. It can take hours for food in a slow cooker to move above the danger zone—and starting with frozen meat delays that process even further.

Recent findings suggest that “The appliance heats food slowly, and starting with frozen meat means the internal temperature may sit in the ‘danger zone’ for too long,” says chef and dietitian Sharniquia White. “This gives bacteria like Salmonella or E. coli more opportunity to multiply before the food reaches a safe cooking temperature.”.

What happens after eating food that has sat in the danger zone? The consequences vary based on your immune system, the extent of the contamination, and the strains of bacteria present. But none are pleasant, and some may even send you to the hospital.

In a recent development, “Symptoms of food-borne illness can include nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and fever,” Koch notes. “You can experience the effects of food-borne illness within a few minutes to days after consuming a load of harmful pathogens or bacteria.”.

In a recent development, cooking frozen meat on the “low” setting of your slow cooker increases the time it spends in the danger zone, but the risk is present regardless. “The 'high' setting reduces the amount of time food spends at unsafe temperatures, but still doesn’t fully eliminate the risk when starting with frozen meat,” says White.

The ingredients you're using can also increase your risk. “Larger, denser cuts (like roasts or whole poultry) take longer to thaw and heat evenly, so they pose a greater risk of staying at unsafe temperatures for extended periods,” White explains.

It has been revealed that smaller pieces may thaw faster, but that doesn't necessarily make them safe to cook from frozen. White explains that ground meat is “particularly risky” because of the way it's processed, so it should be cooked thoroughly.

“I feed three young children at my home, so in my opinion, I wouldn't chance cooking frozen meat, no matter the size, in a slow cooker,” Koch states.

Sources indicate that the answer is simple: thaw your meat before turning on your slow cooker. But your ideal method depends on how much time you have.

The safest, easiest, and least involved thawing method is to put your frozen meat in the fridge. The cold temperature of your refrigerator lets your food defrost gently without entering the danger zone.

It has been revealed that our editors recommend placing the meat on a plate or baking sheet to collect any juices and avoid contaminating other food in your fridge. This process can take anywhere from a couple of hours to a couple of days, depending on the cut of meat. “This requires some thought and effort, but in the long run it's worth your safety,” Koch notes.

Industry observers note that no time for that? No problem. You can thaw meat faster by submerging it in cold water in a leakproof bag, changing the water every 30 minutes, or defrosting it in the microwave, though the latter can compromise the meat's texture. Both methods require cooking the meat immediately afterward. “Once thawed, meat should go directly into the slow cooker,” White explains.

It all takes a little extra effort and planning, but it's worth it to avoid getting sick from your slow cooker dinner.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pavlova is essentially a massive meringue that melts in your mouth. We top our version with whipped cream and fresh berries for an airy and fruity bite that will keep you coming back bite after bite. It may look like a complicated dessert made by only the best chefs, but it's surprisingly easy to make! You just need some patience. The key to perfection is drying it out, which requires you to leave it in a (turned-off) oven overnight after it bakes.

If you’re looking for something a bit more festive, check out our Christmas wreath pavlova for a holiday spin on the classic.

Sources indicate that arrange a rack in the center of the oven; preheat to 300°. In a large bowl, beat egg whites with a large pinch of salt on medium-high speed with a handheld mixer (or in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment) until foamy, which should take about one minute.

While beating, slowly add sugar and beat until meringue is thick and glossy, which should take about 7 minutes. Beat in vinegar, cornstarch, and vanilla until well combined.

Pile the meringue in the center of a parchment-lined baking sheet. Using a spatula or spoon, spread the mixture into an 8" circle. Make a small well in the center.

Sources indicate that transfer to the oven, and immediately reduce the oven temperature to 250°. Bake the meringue until set but still white, which should take about an hour. Turn off the oven and let the pavlova cool completely in the oven for at least 2 hours and up to overnight. Transfer cooled pavlova to a platter.

Top with whipped cream and berries.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Store the unassembled pavlova in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days, keeping it away from humidity. Once topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit, refrigerate and enjoy within a day, as the meringue will soften over time.

With Grand Theft Auto VI, Rockstar Bet $1.5B That Humans Could Make a Better Game Than AI

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that somewhere in the far north of Leonida, Grand Theft Auto VI’s fictional take on Florida, a robbery is taking place.
  • In a recent development, A thunderstorm has recently rolled through this area and the tarmac steams as sunlight knifes through the clouds.
  • Dozens of impromptu moments like this stud GTA6, a video game that makes you feel like one entity among many rather than the spoiled V.I.P.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that somewhere in the far north of Leonida, Grand Theft Auto VI’s fictional take on Florida, a robbery is taking place. This much is unsurprising. Crime is baked into the title of the series, which began in 1997 and, despite its thick American accent, is still predominantly made in Scotland. But Jason and Lucia, the young, beautiful Bonnie and Clyde who together share the role of protagonists in GTA VI, are not the ones committing this crime. Rather, a grizzled biker hangs from the second-floor window of a locked bar, throwing valuables down to his accomplice on the street.

In a recent development, A thunderstorm has recently rolled through this area and the tarmac steams as sunlight knifes through the clouds. It’s Leonida-muggy. Patches of sweat swell beneath Jason’s arms as he takes in the scene. The bikers notice you watching and ask, politely, considering the circumstances, if you could fuck off. A choice presents itself: clamber back on your stolen motorbike and continue your road trip, or insert yourself into this micro-drama and take a principled stand on behalf of concerned citizens everywhere (then take the loot for yourself, of course).

Dozens of impromptu moments like this stud GTA6, a video game that makes you feel like one entity among many rather than the spoiled V.I.P. around whom everything has been artfully arranged. Most video games flatter the player by making them the centre of the virtual universe, the cog on which all the digital clockwork turns. What is extraordinary about Vice City and its surrounding area is how much of the world appears to trundle on without needing your presence or input.

These moments are made possible by dozens of interlocking systems built by dozens of discrete teams. An entire Los-Angeles-based team worked on the personalities and behaviors of the thousands of people who inhabit Vice City; the bar’s interior was meticulously set-dressed to suggest the lives and tastes of its proprietors and patrons, while the biker’s dialogue and reactions to your choices were written, cast and performed. The weather, too, is restless: cloud and rain move across the world, dynamically changing light and mood. This tableaux, which only a small percentage of players may ever encounter, has not been staged like a scene in a play but rather cultivated in what amounts to the world’s most expensive Petri dish.

Since 1984, when Elite first used procedural generation to conjure an entire galaxy on a computer screen, game designers have learned to produce universes from scant technological resources. But in the era of procedural generation, scale is almost routine; the harder, more costly work is making an expanse feel handmade and coherent. GTA VI manages both, with districts populated by distinct communities and social strata, each shaped by decades of imagined history. It reveals a kind of detail and thoughtfulness that A.I. has yet to reproduce convincingly—and perhaps never will.

The game’s lavishness is not only visible in the rain, the sweat and the individual strands of hair falling across Lucia’s shoulders, but also in the hundreds, perhaps thousands, of diversions away from the criminal grind. For example, Jason and Lucia can take time out from planning a heist to compete in illegal street races for prize money, enter dirt-bike scrambles or race stock cars in a stadium. You can become a hunter, choosing a rifle to suit your quarry so as not to ruin its pelt; start drone racing, streaking through abandoned buildings in an FPV headset; or dive for treasure among old shipwrecks, dodging both the circling sharks, and the authorities who want to check your license.

A compelling main story runs through the game, with missions that leave room for different approaches: you might play as a careful shooter, aiming to wound rather than kill, or as a less discerning one. The couple, so artfully written and performed, offer vivid points of entry into the world as you guide them from relative poverty towards financial security that, perhaps, might allow them to build a family life beyond crime. But much of the joy comes from straying from the main path.

To that end the game makes room for long, meandering drives across the country and peaceful early-morning flights over mountain ranges. You can spend a sleepy afternoon with a scenic view, peering through dollar-a-minute binoculars. Many of these diversions appeared in the studio’s earlier games, but here they feel newly vivid, rendered with extraordinary fidelity. The smaller encounters are just as memorable. Happen upon a possum at night and it might play dead on the tarmac. In a thrift store, you can while away assembling fits worthy of a Ralph Lauren vintage buyer; at a 24-hour nightclub, you can dance until sunrise, before emerging blinking into the dawn while wondering, as Kanye once put it, if they’ve got cabs still. (Of course they do: you can summon one in an instant from your virtual phone).

Industry observers note that this is lavish game-making on an unprecedented scale. The irony, however, is that GTA VI arrives at a moment when other studios are bleeding staff (if they survive at all) and the cost of making games at anywhere close to this level continues to rise precipitously. In one industry survey published this month, a third of respondents noted they had been laid off in the past two years; more than half of those laid off had yet to find fresh work—a stark picture of the ongoing insecurity across the industry. In the early 2010s, game budgets fell between $30 and $70 million. McKinsey puts the current cost of a blockbuster game production at $200 million to $500 million. At these prices, few can pay to play.

Even amid the union-busting allegations (which Rockstar denies; an employment tribunal is ongoing), the company has retained much of its long-serving talent between major releases. That continuity gives it a store of institutional knowledge that is hard to preserve when studios expand and contract around individual projects. Key members of GTA VI’s leadership have worked together for decades. The studio also has a clear commercial advantage over its closest creative peers: Naughty Dog, creator of the Uncharted and The Last of Us series, and CD Projekt Red, creator of The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077. Their story-led games can dominate a moment, but their stories conclude when the credits roll.

In a recent development, after players finished Grand Theft Auto V’s story, by contrast, they could continue to inhabit its world through GTA Online, joining others in an ever-replenishing sandbox of play. A leak of Rockstar data suggested that GTA Online averaged about $9.6 million a week between September 2025 and April 2026—roughly $42 million a month. Rockstar is owned by Take-Two, and there is no evidence that GTA Online’s astonishing revenue was entirely funneled into GTA VI. But a game generating revenue year after year gives its parent a durable source of income, justifying artisanal-style work. These factors make Grand Theft Auto VI’s scale and fidelity exceptionally difficult for any rival to match.

It has been revealed that that challenge is something even Rockstar’s former leaders have had to reckon with. Leslie Benzies—who for years was one of the three creative leaders on Rockstar projects alongside Sam and Dan Houser (of the trio, only Sam remains at the organization)—founded Build a Rocket Boy, which raised more than $300 million before releasing MindsEye. The game’s troubled launch was followed by mass redundancies and, in September 2026, a slide into administration. The lesson seems clear. Money alone cannot buy the infrastructure, expertise and returning audience that have allowed Rockstar to build this world at extraordinary length.

According to recent reports, in a game filled with enticing luxuries, from expensive shoes to glinting supercars, the visible human hand is, in this dawning age of AI abundance, the rarest luxury of all in Leonida. You can leave the bikers to their robbery: clouds drift on, the tarmac dries. The world keeps its own time. Making that unforced life cohere took years of work across many teams, and required a collective attention to every detail. With budgets rising and studios closing, perhaps no other company could afford such a wager. Leonida is a miracle of craft—and a monument to a form of game-making the wider industry can no longer sustain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that “Melodramatic” barely grasps the intense emotional roller coaster of The Hunting Wives. The Netflix soap opera/erotic thriller introduced the world to the small town of Maple Brook, Texas, where the world revolves around a small group of eccentric, gun-toting divas who disproportionately find themselves at the center of sinful controversies that range from infidelity to murder.

Inspired by May Cobb’s novel by the same name, The Hunting Wives follows Sophie O’Neil (Brittany Snow), a bright-eyed transplant from Massachusetts who moves to Maple Brook with her husband, Graham (Evan Jonigkeit), and young son. This is partly because Sophie accidentally killed someone during a night of drunk driving. But now, Graham works for Jed (Dermot Mulroney), the richest man in town, who is gearing up for a gubernatorial run. His wife, Margo Banks (Malin Akerman), is the hypnotizing beating heart of this small town, along with her crew of strong-willed “hunting wives.” Upon meeting her, Sophie is immediately bewitched by her stoic demeanor and magnetic charm.

It has been revealed that margo’s inner circle includes several shit-talking, heavy-drinking wives who spend their days gossiping or shooting boars. Two of Margo’s small army rank above the rest: Jill Thompson (Katie Lowes), the pastor’s wife who loves her 18-year-old basketball prodigy son, Brad (George Ferrier), a bit too much, and Callie, the sheriff’s wife, who is fiercely (delusionally?) loyal to Margo. Margo and Callie’s love is very much not platonic, but it’s repeatedly jeopardized, especially because Margo is enamored with Sophie. In short, Callie hates (and I mean hates) Sophie.

To understand the show, one thing needs to be made abundantly clear: Everyone is horny, and anything is fair game. Or almost anything. At the center of Maple Brook’s salacious tangle of relationships is Jed and Margo’s (mostly) open marriage. The two of them can sleep with as many women as they want, and I mean only women (a misogynistic arrangement, yes, but this is Deep South Texas, after all). This allows Jed as many trysts as he wants and permits Margo’s secret romance with Callie. This rule, however, doesn’t really stop her from doing whatever she wants when she wants. This is deadly apparent because she’s full-blown romantically involved with (checks notes) her friend Jill’s teenage son, Brad.

Saddle up, we’re only getting started.

Recent findings suggest that the first part of The Hunting Wives finds thrills in socialites at each other’s throats. They toss dagger eyes, pair them with biting insults, and let lust dictate most (if not all) of their decisions. Then, a real tragedy rattles the town. Brad’s real (age-appropriate) girlfriend, the sweet Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe), is found shot in the head in the forest near the town lake. Many viable suspects live in this crime-ridden town: Pete (Paul Teal), the youth pastor who cares too much about his teens; Jill, viciously protective of her son; and Margo, who, as I mentioned, is sleeping with teenage Brad. The cops, however, only find signs pointing to the unassuming Sophie O’Neil, who spent the night at Margo’s nearby the night before and whose gun was confirmed as the murder weapon. (Uh-oh!).

The night of Abby Jackson’s murder, she leaves the lake party mad at Brad, who failed to show up because, well, he’s having sex with Margo. As the audience, we also learn that two prime suspects roam nearby: An angry Jill left the house to confront Abby, and creepy Pastor Pete parked his car nearby where he was … masturbating to a photo of Abby. But Margo invites Sophie over to her lake house for a night of fun. Without telling Sophie, Margot also invites Brad and his friend, Jamie (Chosen Jacobs), another 18-year-old who has the hots for Sophie—what a disaster! That night, Margo and Sophie share a kiss during Spin the Bottle, sparking one of the most co-manipulative relationships in TV history. On top of it all, they mix Xanax and alcohol, so no one remembers anything. This is troubling when Sophie wakes up alone on the dock with no memory and no gun.

Industry observers note that we know Sophie’s gun was used to kill Abby—and she certainly had opportunity. But she had no motive whatsoever. Margo, on the other hand, has all three; Abby discovered Brad and Margo’s affair and threatened to expose it (an affair that, of course, had yielded an unplanned pregnancy and a subsequent abortion). And, in a frantic attempt to keep her wealthy lifestyle intact, she shoots Abby. But that was only the beginning. Margo first attempts to frame Sophie for the murder, but because she holds a soft spot for her, she instead decides to frame Jill, planting Abby’s phone in her house and twisting the story to her liking.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, it’s essential to talk about what happened to Abby’s mother, Starr, who is often bullied by the popular clique of high-powered women. After Abby dies, Starr thinks Brad is the culprit, having seen the two of them engaged in a fight, but she changes her mind after she’s incorrectly told Abby’s had an abortion (it was Margo), and she thinks that Jill killed Abby to protest Brad. That’s when Starr, in a fury, drives to Jill’s with a shotgun in tow, only to get mowed down by the gun-toting pastor’s wife in an act of self-defense.

Jill emerges victorious from her spar with Starr, but it doesn’t last long. The cops start looking at her as the prime suspect because she was the last incoming call on Abby’s phone (and she had a motive). Margo, obviously knowing that’s not the case, accompanies Callie to confront Jill anyway, only to find Starr dead in the kitchen. That’s when Jill pulls a gun on them (this is crazy, I know), and Callie shoots first, killing her. This is also, in some way, a twisted act of love.

As all the shooting is going on, an off-duty cop follows a red herring in the form of Pastor Pete. (Yes, everyone is a little evil in Maple Brook, but he might be the most sinister resident of them all.) Deputy Wanda Salazar (Karen Rodriguez) has a feeling that the pastor isn’t who he notes he is and is hiding a dark past. Thinking he is Abby’s murderer, she chases him down, only to find that he’s kidnapped two other girls, Kaycee and Nina, hauling them in a trailer behind his car. What the hell is in the water in this town!?

It has been revealed that by the eighth episode, it seems Sophie has perhaps drunk too much of this Maple Brook water. She pieces together that Margo is the killer—and that she manipulated the situation to frame her for murder. Instead of going straight to the authorities (like any normal person might), she confronts Margo. This, of course, gives Margo enough time to alert her crazy, crack-smoking brother Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), who pops up as a nuisance throughout the series. Taking on the role of a protective older brother, Kyle tries to run Sophie off the road and intimidate her. What does she do? Run him over and kill him … so, no use going to the authorities anymore. In true Maple Brook fashion, she hides the body instead. And, yes, after all that, we’re ready for season 2, because now everyone’s a killer.

We will see what’s next for this sinister Texan town on November 26.

Vegan Stuffing

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, listen, we all know that stuffing is the best part of Thanksgiving dinner, but because of the butter, eggs, and chicken broth that usually go into classic stuffing, it's a dish that vegans can't always enjoy—until now! We created a stuffing that's so delicious, you might even be convinced to make a few of your other holiday classics into vegan Thanksgiving versions.

Start your stuffing off by preheating the oven to 200° and slicing the bread into roughly 1” cubes. Spread the cubes in a single layer on a large baking sheet and bake for about 20 minutes, until the bread is nice and crisp.

In a recent development, remove the bread from the oven and turn the temperature up to 350°. Grease a 13” x 9” baking dish with cooking spray and heat oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add onion to the skillet and cook for about 5 minutes until lightly charred in some spots, then add the celery and garlic and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until the celery starts to turn translucent. Pour in the vegetable stock and scrape up any browned bits—this is where all the flavor is. Season with salt and pepper.

Mix the bread cubes and chopped herbs in the vegetable stock mixture until well combined, then transfer to the prepared baking dish.

Cover the dish tightly with aluminum foil and place it in the oven to bake for 40 minutes. Carefully remove the foil and continue baking for another 35 minutes, until the stuffing is golden brown and crisp on top.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Looking for more vegan holiday inspo? Whip up our cauliflower stuffing for a low-carb option, or try out our vegetarian mushroom gravy or vegan mashed potatoes to truly complete your spread!

It has been revealed that any leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. You can also prepare this dish ahead of time, as it’s the kind of dish that we think tastes even better after sitting for a day.

#146173. 15 Best Beard Oils for Taming Your Stubborn Facial Hair

15 Best Beard Oils for Taming Your Stubborn Facial Hair

📅 08 Dec 2016 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that so, you've realized.
  • It has been revealed that I’d go so far as to rank beard oil as the second most crucial beard care product, just after beard trimmers.
  • In a recent development, for the longest time, I thought of Honest Amish as “that Amazon beard oil,” given its enormous popularity on the e-tailer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that so, you've realized. Growing a beard was only the beginning: Now you’ve gotta give it some love. Thankfully, the best beard oil will keep that sculpted scruff feeling great! And not just for you, either, because the right beard oil leaves your skin glowing—and stops your facial hair from annoying any partner who gets close to it. Great beard oils also keep coarse hair from getting brittle and wiry, and soften your beard so you’re not scratching your neck or dealing with beard dandruff (yes, it exists). All that from just a couple drops of wonder oil.

It has been revealed that I’d go so far as to rank beard oil as the second most crucial beard care product, just after beard trimmers. And it’s a close second. Because whether you keep your facial hair at a precise 24-hour stubble, go full hermit-mode, or stay somewhere in between, a beard oil does irreplaceable work. (The kind you can’t replace with any old moisturizer or conditioner.) So, if you’re tired of flyaways, coarse beard hair, dandruff, or itchiness, these GQ-tested and approved beard oils will turn your scruff into fluff. Promise.

In a recent development, for the longest time, I thought of Honest Amish as “that Amazon beard oil,” given its enormous popularity on the e-tailer. (At the time of writing, we’re talking nearly 30,000 reviews and a 4.5-star rating.) And often, I'll intentionally seek out an alternative to these Amazon-beloved grooming products—if only because it feels like the equivalent of recommending Applebee's to an out-of-towner. But this time, well: Welcome to Applebee's.

Recent findings suggest that frankly, I couldn't find a better beard oil. Not only is Honest Amish cost-effective (at the second-best price-per-ounce on my list), but the brand nailed the blend. It's a pure oil recipe (no non-oil ingredients), with seven carrier oils and seven essential oils that give it an earthy scent and help tone the skin beneath your bushel. It absorbs fast, works great to smooth down flyaways, relax stiff bristles, and battle both dry skin and flake-prone beards. And did I mention the value? Six bucks per ounce is a steal.

Industry observers note that to be clear, I only use Honest Amish on my beard, largely because I'm not a fan of using any essential oils on bare skin—I particularly find that pumpkin seed oil (a key ingredient here) can be slightly pore-clogging on acne-prone skin. That mentioned: I count myself as acne-prone and haven't had issues with Honest Amish, so I'm probably being over-cautious. It's really just that good.

Despite the name Beardbrand, this company's product line covers the whole body, with a focus on multi-tasking grooming products like dual washes, all-purpose balms, and this utilitarian oil. You'll catch me using it on my hands, elbows, and hair—whether for a dash of shine (to offset a matte hair product) or a protective coat against frizz and humidity. But Beardbrand's Utility Oil is on this list because it works beautifully in the beard.

Recent findings suggest that sure, it's a touch heavier than some other oils—but that also makes it a terrific pre-shave lubricant. It's crucial to note that no matter which “flavor” you choose, this oil has a strong dash of fragrance. They're all good, but I'm partial to the brand's latest Bold Fortune scent, which oozes a sexy combo of leather, oud, and tobacco. (And pro-tip: The brand's utility wash has the same come-hither scent, if you want to double down.).

In a recent development, horace's beard oil will make a lot of you happy, though for different reasons. For those overwhelmed by scents—particularly artificial ones—you'll appreciate that its got the subtlest of aromas. I'm partial to the Lemon & Mint one, which reads as “fresh" and never overwhelms. For those looking to stay away from chemicals, Horace's formula is 99% natural—and the 1% is a synthetic grapeseed oil, not something with 12 syllables, which I'm fine with.

Sources indicate that the brand gets bonus marks for its easily-understood ingredients labels, which break down these details and err on the side of much-appreciated transparency. Finally, if you're on the fence about beard oils, Horace will make you a believer. It absorbs fast, gives a pinch of shine, and makes just enough difference in terms of taming, moisturizing, and softening that you'll see why a beard oil makes sense.

In the grooming world, Jack Black (the brand) has earned its own fanbase, thanks in large part to one product—the signature Jack Black beard oil. Apply just a few drops and it immediately goes to work softening coarse and brittle facial hair, and without an overpowering fragrance that will distract you all day long. It's one of the most popular beard oils on Amazon, but don't hold that against it. While it softens and adds shine, this oil also delivers a dose of antioxidants and vitamins from natural ingredients such as brown algae and rosemary.

It also uses a unique blend of oils with the subtlest whiff of melon fragrance. Instead of the usual suspects (jojoba, avocado, sunflower seed), this product uses Kalahari melon oil, marula oil, and plum oil, which moisturize your facial hair and skin on contact. Because these oils are all fast-absorbing (my beard hair soaks it up like a sponge), they make this product much less greasy than other beard oils, giving it a more premium feel.

According to recent reports, I test literally hundreds of grooming products a year, and I'm so intimately acquainted with brands fresh and old that I often think about them based on their best product. For Pura d'Or, it's this organic beard oil. It's the best value on this list, at $3 per fluid ounce. Given how quickly you can go through beard oil—just think, if you're applying up to twice a day, that dollar-per-ounce math becomes crucial. So, in addition to being my budget pick, this also gets my recommendation as the best beard oil for major beards.

It has been revealed that of course, it's only crucial if the formula measures up—and here, it does. There are two carrier oils, argan and jojoba, along with a bit of grapefruit peel and some sandalwood essential oil for both a natural scent and a touch of antimicrobial powers. It's a great beard oil for anyone, no matter how big your bank account, but if you're bearding on a budget, you'll appreciate how much goodness Pura d'Or packs into a few bucks.

According to recent reports, blind Barber's tonka-tinged oil is wonderful for the guy who wants to moisturize skin and whiskers with the same product. It wears extremely light—so much so that my oily skin barely registers its presence—and I find its carrier-oil-centric and shea-butter-forward formula especially comforting on the skin. It should be noted that this formula includes artificial perfume, so fragrance-averse individuals should steer clear. But for those of us who want a special scent, a flake-free beard, and soothed skin, Blind Barber's beard oil does it all.

While I'd use most of the above options as both a hair oil and a beard oil, Aesop's is one where I think of it as a hair oil first and foremost. It brings control without making things look greasy, while trapping moisture and stopping frizz. I'll use it in short hair to tame down the sides, in medium lengths (mixed with a cream or clay) for added shine, or in long hair to prevent split ends. Then, once my hair's settled up, I'll run my hands through my beard afterward. So, if you want a great hair oil with beard benefits, Aesop's is the winner.

Since the beginning of the men's grooming boom, I've been waiting for the big designer fashion houses to start catering to guys with facial hair. For now, Tom Ford's beard oil stands alone. So, how does the designer oil stack up against our everyday favorites? After trying it out, I can tell you it’s better as a fragrance than a beard oil, but the scent alone earns it a spot in this guide.

The tobacco vanilla fragrance is much more sophisticated than what we’re used to seeing, or smelling, in this space. The scent puts an emphasis on vanilla, and you just need one or two pumps for full coverage. Considering the price and the name on the bottle, we were shocked to find this oil comes in a plastic pump bottle, but that fragrance. If you want to buy beard oil as a gift, this premium conditioning oil is a step up over your average Amazon brand, even if it doesn't soften coarse hair as well as some of our other options.

It has been revealed that if you have sensitive skin—or if you're afraid of your beard oil clashing with your daily cologne—then Marlowe makes one of the only fragrance-free beard oils. Most beard oil formulas contain both essential oils and some type of perfume oil (or, parfum, for my fellow ingredients detectives), which can be risky for your skin, follicles, and pores, so it’s nice to have an option for acne-prone and sensitive skin types.

Sources indicate that this beard oil couldn’t be simpler—and I mean that in a good way. Marlowe No. 143 has an all-oil formula and just four ingredients: safflower seed oil, sunflower seed oil, corn oil, and soybean oil. That’s it. Considering the average beauty product contains up to a dozen ingredients we can’t even pronounce, it’s a refreshing change. Although, I have to say, if you want the softest possible beard, Honest Amish also makes a fragrance-free oil.

Industry observers note that most guys use beard oil to tame flyaways. But what if you want the thickest, fullest beard possible? In that case, I’d recommend reaching for Bevel’s oil. This brand makes skin and hair products for Black men, but anyone with coarse or curly hair can benefit from their products. GQ contributor Timothy Beck Werth reports that this oil gave him a thicker-looking beard without excess frizz, which isn't easy to do. (BTW, that’s as much as you can expect from any beard oil, so please don’t fall for the “beard growth serums” you’ll find all over the internet.).

Recent findings suggest that for parched facial hair, the grapeseed, macadamia, jojoba, and argan oil will condition your beard and add a healthy shine. For beneath the scruff, the avocado and primrose oil with soothe your skin without clogging up your pores and follicles. Werth says this beard oil instantly softened his facial hair, and he also liked the sweeter smell of the macadamia-based formula. Most beard oils opt for woodsy fragrances, and the more subtle scent profile here is a nice surprise, he explains.

Anthony’s conditioning beard oil is a 2-in-1 product—a pre-shave oil and regular beard oil. That approach can be risky, since a lot of multipurpose products try to be everything and succeed at nothing, but luckily that’s not the case here. If you regularly cycle between clean-shaven, stubble, and full-on lighthouse keeper, then you can still use this product daily. As a pre-shave oil, it moisturizes the skin and softens facial hair for a smoother shave with fewer morning-after red bumps. As a beard oil, it hydrates, then locks in that moisture so your beard stays soft and shiny all day. I found the consistency to be somewhere in between a leave-in conditioner gel and a traditional oil, making it thicker and less messy to apply.

The oil also has an herbaceous, minty fragrance that’s so refreshing it feels like aromatherapy every time you run it through your hair. That’s because the formula is full of ingredients that smell good, feel good, and actually help your skin and hair. It uses carrier oils like soybean and castor to deliver skin-pleasing and antimicrobial botanicals such as rosemary, basil, tea tree oil, eucalyptus, and spearmint. And on the hydration front, calendula and olive oil nourish your whiskers into their softest, fluffiest selves. Because of the more complex fragrance and ingredients profile, this wouldn’t be my pick for guys with sensitive skin. Still, it’s a multi-functional serum you’ll look forward to using every day.

Lots of beard oils promise to get flyaways under control, yet those rogue hairs keep popping up. So, what do you do? Instead of trying yet another oil, try reaching for a product that’s more of a leave-in conditioner for your beard. We’ve previously praised Zeus’s beard brushes, but the California-based brand also makes a beard serum that deserves a spot in your bathroom cabinet. I love that this beard oil has the simplest possible ingredients list: sweet almond oil, soybean oil, argan seed oil, trihydroxystearin, avocado oil, and fragrance.

The only multi-syllable ingredient there is a simple thickening agent, which gives this refined beard oil a gel-like consistency. That thicker formula will also put flyaways in their place. The very subtle fragrance is more Mediterranean than winter pine forest (we tested the Verbena Lime version), but you can also opt for a fragrance-free formula if you have sensitive skin or allergies. The plastic bottle uses an air pump, letting you get every last drop of oil. For clean freaks who hate the messiness and spillage that always comes with beard oil application, this is another bonus.

Industry observers note that tired of being left out of couple’s skincare night just because those stupid sheet masks won’t hold onto your glorious beard? Cardon’s got you, boo. Actually, this bead oil hack is perfect for guys who only sparingly use beard oil on an as-needed basis.

The bamboo and charcoal sheet mask is specially shaped for guys with beards, and each mask comes with a dose of beard oil made with argan and jojoba oil. In the Venn diagram of Korean skincare and beard care products, this sheet mask-beard oil duo is the tiny, microscopic bit of overlap in the middle.

The best best oil should support your skin and your beard, and Baxter of California's sweet-smelling oil doesn't sacrifice one for the other. In his guide to the best beard care products, GQ's Timothy Beck Werth stated that “In our testing, no beard oil absorbs as quickly or spreads as evenly as this one.” Squalane helps nourish the most overlooked skin on your face, while avocado oil, vitamin E, and botanical extracts smooth out your beard.

Industry observers note that as with anything you put on your skin, the ingredients are what matter most. And with beard oils, there are two categories of ingredients: carrier oils and essential oils. No two ingredients will perform exactly the same. Some will help with very specific situations or conditions; some may actively aggravate your skin. Essential oils in particular can aggravate skin if used by themselves. So, consider the following carrier oils and essential oils, favored both by myself and Alyssa Bachowski, a senior barber at Fellow Barber’s Williamsburg, NYC barbershop.

Carrier oils—often vegetable and see oils—make up the bulk of these beard oil formulas, bringing beard nourishment and skin hydration. The most popular carrier oils are argan oil and jojoba oil (both of which Bachowski recommends), though there are dozens of varieties, from castor to marula to grape seed oils. They're usually unscented, though some—like coconut oil—may carry an aroma. Because carrier oils make up the “base” of the oil, they should be among the first to appear in a product's formula or list of ingredients.

“Jojoba oil is non-comedogenic, which means it will not clog your pores. It is also a lighter oil that is absorbent, so it won't just sit on top of the hair and give you a greasy appearance,” Bachowski notes. Along with argan oil, you’re going to see a lot of jojoba oil in most popular beard oil blends.

It has been revealed that “Argan oil is filled with a ton of vitamins and minerals, as well as linoleic acid, sterolins, and squalene. All of these aid in protecting and keeping your skin and beard healthy,” Bachowski says.

Recent findings suggest that “Castor oil is known for promoting beard hair growth,” states Bachowski. It’s hypothetically the best beard-growth oil of the crew, because it acts like a vitamin for your strands—though there's more on that below in the FAQs. But don't expect it to grow more hairs, or thicker hairs. Castor oil does have a smoke-and-mirrors benefit, at least. “It is a heavier oil and dark in color, so it can give the appearance of a denser beard on men with dark facial hair,” Bachowski says.

Grape seed oil can help tone down your skin's oil production, and is extremely moisturizing for scruff and skin alike.

Rich in fatty acids, this is a frontrunner for “most nourishing oil” for your skin and whiskers.

Yes, shea butter is in fact a carrier oil, and it has supremely moisturizing properties that make it great for detangling scraggly beards and softening stiff hairs.

It has been revealed that essential oils are distillations from more potent sources, and they tend to be additive—and active—ingredients in a beard oil. These oils are typically extracted through steaming methods, and their range of benefits can include antimicrobial properties, oil-toning abilities, and soothing superpowers. Typically, any natural fragrance in a beard oil will come from essential oils. But pure essential oils can be extremely damaging to the skin.

“You should not apply pure essential oil to a beard—it will do the opposite of what you are trying to achieve,” Bachowski says. “These [pure oils] are not good for your beard nor your skin. as they can be irritating and harmful. Essential oils can cause dryness, itchiness, and redness—and some people may have allergic reactions to them.” This is exactly why you want beard oils from trusted, tested brand.

Bachowski likes cedarwood oil for its naturally astringent properties. “It helps cleanse the pores and prevent ingrown hairs,” she adds. It also adds a natural fragrance.

“Sandalwood has anti-inflammatory properties that help reduce any skin irritation,” Bachowski says of this deliciously scented oil.

Recent findings suggest that lavender helps calm inflammation and redness, says Bachowski. Plus it brings lavender's soothing scent.

This antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, oil-toning ingredient is terrific for acne-prone faces and oily skin types.

Along with its refreshing scent, grapefruit peel oil helps nourish and detangle.

As GQ's lead grooming product reviewer, I've tried just about every beard oil in the biz. The ones chosen for this roundup excel at protecting and moisturizing both skin and hair, with minimal risk for things like inverse reactions and blemishes. They absorb cleanly, unless they expressly choose not to (like those which expressly use silicone), and they smell terrific (with both natural and artificially scented options). I've tested beard oils for a decade, on a beard that's been long, short, and everything in between. I've also scoured online reviews to confirm that these products are backed by throngs of loyal fans, whose collective opinion echoes my own experiences.

What is the best beard oil according to GQ?

It has been revealed that with more than a decade of testing beard oils under his belt, GQ’s expert tester chose Honest Amish as the best beard oil. And 29,000 Amazon shoppers have rated this same product 4.5 out of 5 stars.

What is the difference between beard balm vs. oil?

In a recent development, both beard balm and beard oil are both terrific for facial hair—but they don't do the same job. Beard balm is optimal for taming and styling facial hair, especially at medium and longer lengths. Beard oil provides less control over the shape and style, but is excellent at softening and conditioning the hairs and the skin underneath (preventing beard itch, beard dandruff, and split ends).

Sources indicate that after using a beard wash, most beard oils are applied the same way: “Start off with 2-3 drops in the palm of your hand,” notes Bachowski. “Rub it into your hands so that it is evenly distributed from fingertips to the heel of your hand. Start by rubbing the oil with your fingertips onto the skin beneath the beard hair, then eventually working the oil from root to tip of the actual beard. Make sure to also apply oil to your neck and cheeks where you may have shaved or trimmed as well. If you feel like the 2-3 drops wasn't enough based on the length or density of your beard, apply another 2-3 drops.”.

How do you prevent beard dandruff?

Recent findings suggest that preventing beard dandruff starts with changing your skincare regimen. Namely, introducing exfoliation and moisturizing products that can get past a thick nest of facial hair. For exfoliation, look for physical scrubs (even a beard brush will work). For the best moisturizing effects, be sure to apply beard oil both morning and night. The beard oil will also soften and condition the facial hair to prevent itchiness.

Does beard oil help grow a beard?

No, beard oil is not meant to help beard hair growth, whether that’s to make facial hair thicker or grow faster. To be honest, we don’t know of much that can really change your scruff's density besides a beard transplant and maybe minoxidil. Beard oil is here to make your existing beard hair softer and more cooperative, while also nourishing the skin beneath the beard—skin that’s often prone to dehydration and dandruff. It’s already doing a lot.

Absolutely. Beard oil is a great investment for anyone with facial hair, since it can help soften and tame your scruff while simultaneously moisturizing the skin underneath. This means no more itching, no flyaways, and no beard dandruff.

Alyssa Bachowski is a senior barber at Fellow Barber’s Williamsburg NYC barbershop location.

When the Days of Being Wild Come to an End

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this week, after reading up about the major differences between sea salt and rock salt, I found myself looking at a shot of my mates in an east London restaurant’s smoking area.
  • Industry observers note that it dawned on me that I’ve consciously uncoupled from chaos—an intense long-term relationship that, for many years, I considered an essential part of my personality.
  • I rather romanticized being a bit of a disaster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this week, after reading up about the major differences between sea salt and rock salt, I found myself looking at a shot of my mates in an east London restaurant’s smoking area. My friends looked happy—mildly drunk, joyous, their night still full of possibility—and I felt… hmmm… hard to say what I felt. Not jealous, not one bit, but also not relieved that I was home and dry. Maybe the word is content? Happy enough for them without longing for a sip from the same goblet.

Industry observers note that it dawned on me that I’ve consciously uncoupled from chaos—an intense long-term relationship that, for many years, I considered an essential part of my personality. Anyone who knew me in or around the summer of 2005—the thrifted grandad shirts, the Kate Moss for Topshop skinny jeans—knows I liked a bit of disorder, a grubbiness to the glamour. We dressed to go out, we went out, we laughed and toasted to nothing and smashed our empty glasses down. I would take sunglasses to pre-drinks because any night of the week could bring me the sun on the horizon. My party trick, without a doubt, was stamina. I have done walks of shame, drenched in thick glitter, at three in the afternoon. I wasn’t interested in looking after myself, or my surroundings, or anything that required sustained effort beyond the immediate gratification of the moment. I just needed somewhere to lie flat between merrymakings. I was rootless and selfish in only the way a person with almost zero real responsibilities, who’s still trying to find their way in the world, can be. Sleep was negotiable, meals were incidental. I wasn’t interested in wellness; I just needed a cigarette for the morning; and I don’t remember hydrating once in a decade—I was too busy getting on with things, preferably at speed.

I rather romanticized being a bit of a disaster. I think we all did back then. Blame Pete Doherty. There was something appealing about running on…erm…adrenaline, partying at capacity, being slightly behind on everything else. I mistook a lack of self-preservation for spontaneity and great swathes of disorganization for having a social life. I didn’t want to become one of those people who had everything Filofaxed; those people had missed the point of being alive.

In a recent development, nowadays, weeknights find me with my trotters up in front of Red Dwarf, getting a little laundry done before bed. I’ve developed an unexpected appetite for maintenance: clean, high-thread-count sheets, say, or a handsomely stocked fridge. A house that doesn’t look as though a small twister has blown through, clothes that don’t scream French-robber-cum-mime. Doing a four-step skincare routine and going to sleep at a reasonable hour. Reading a physical book.

I have become a man who likes things to be nice. I find myself taking pleasure in the small, unremarkable business of keeping things (and myself) in working order. There’s a time and place for the extraordinary, for the luxurious. But functioning, clean, and considered is eclipsing my more indulgent peccadillos.

I still like being out for dinner, and I still like bars where every drink is three-parts spirit, but I also like relieving the sitter by 11. I’m out with you; I just think, Wow, that was lovely; and then I leave. There’s no FOMO from the Uber, no twinge of the grass once being greener, of my body once being younger and more readily available for adventure. The cravings were gone, the mind-chatter silenced.

Recent findings suggest that I remain suspicious of people who seem to have turned being alive into an elaborate administrative exercise, a series of panic attacks about microplastics. My personality refuses to revolve around my cortisol levels or “sleep hygiene.” But I am beginning to understand that treating yourself like an afterthought isn’t particularly glamorous. Nor is being permanently exhausted. I don’t think I need to spend the rest of my life recovering from last night.

Fatherhood accelerated this realization because fatherhood accelerates all realizations. There’s another person in my house who has very little interest in whether I’ve had enough sleep, whether I’ve eaten properly. She assumes—fairly reasonably?—the adults are taking care of things. Looking after myself, in turn, becomes less of a personal treat and more of a basic courtesy to the human I created. As a byproduct, I’ve discovered the pleasure of an ordinary day that doesn’t require damage control. I’m not dodging hangovers for the baby, per se, but I also don’t see the fun in keeping watch of a zig-zagging toddler while waiting for the Advil to kick in before your about-last-night apology tour. There’s something in a morning without regret, a house without a domestic backlog, an evening that doesn’t need to be wrung dry for every last drop of excitement.

I’ve finally shed the conviction that being interesting requires a destructive streak. I haven’t become a different person, but I’ve redirected my night energy to a place of comfort. I’ve stopped treating my own life as something I can afford to neglect. Chaos and I are still on speaking terms, obviously; a toddler is the absolute essence of chaos. But I’ve decided one source of chaos—with a strict 7 p.m. bedtime—is enough for now. The party isn’t over, I’m just focused on the mornings after.

The Art of the Winter Layer

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor.
  • Like any specialized skill set, winter layering is one that must be continually practiced and perfected, lest your talents wane.
  • That said, even the most adept artist is nothing without an arsenal of trusted creative tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Like any specialized skill set, winter layering is one that must be continually practiced and perfected, lest your talents wane. It’s not as easy as throwing on a pair of cashmere leggings and a coordinating hoodie—that’s only the beginning. From there, it takes a careful curation of hero pieces (like puffer jackets and parkas), as well as a cast of supporting details (hats, gloves, and high-performance footwear), to layer effectively and aesthetically in the harshest conditions.

That said, even the most adept artist is nothing without an arsenal of trusted creative tools. And in these bitter temps, you’ll want to reach for the best, which essentially means any piece of gear with The North Face’s iconic rectangular logo attached to it. The storied brand has dominated the outdoor space for decades, having perfected the art of elevated style at elevated altitudes.

According to recent reports, as we head into the chilliest season of the year, look to The North Face’s vast selection of dependable staples for all your layering needs. Designed both for performance and appearances, these pieces are in it for the long run.

In a recent development, whether painting or dressing, it’s essential to start any creative endeavor with a blank canvas made of quality materials. A good base should be versatile and simple to pair with a host of helpful staples. Long-sleeve tees, cashmere turtlenecks, and crewneck sweatshirts, for example, are all good jumping-off points.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking for a high-performance piece with enough style power to stand on its own, we recommend the Women’s Chabot 2.0 Mock-Neck. This cozy layering top offers the same reliable comfort of a traditional insulated thermal with a few modern updates. Though understated by design, its delightfully oversized fit and a funky waffle knit texture make the basic feel intentional and interesting.

For a closer-fitting base, the Women’s Golden Ridge Ribbed Long-Sleeve Tee layers easily under other pieces. Its slim fit and ribbed texture give this practical layer a polished look, while thumbholes at the cuffs add a functional detail. Bonus points for the tee’s anti-odor technology that helps keep the fabric feeling fresh.

Women’s Golden Ridge Ribbed Long-Sleeve Tee.

After you’ve selected the first layer, the next stop should be your coat closet. This is where you’ll select the hero of your look. While each piece of the layering puzzle is uniquely notable, the power jacket is a non-negotiable. The right iteration should supply a thick layer of warmth, while also doing its part to make the outfit, as a whole, feel cohesive.

Recent findings suggest that those who crave a more subdued winter aesthetic will love the classic appeal of the Women’s Arctic Bomber. The waterproof winter jacket boasts all the utility of a parka, with the sleek design details most commonly found in trend-focused outerwear. In four comforting colorways, this winter coat is an insulation powerhouse in a chic, wearable package.

Look to the Women’s Hydrenalite Down Jacket for a more classic puffer. This work-horse is a versatile down layer that can be slipped on at any time to keep you warm for any duration that you spend outdoors, whether you are on the mountain or running around town.

For the more artistically inclined, try the Women’s Yumiori Off Peak Full Zip Jacket. This fleece outer layer offers unfailing warmth and a distinctly sporty flavor. Its two-tone color palette, meanwhile, adds a fun, whimsical feel to the utilitarian, zip-up-style silhouette.

Women’s Hydrenalite Down Jacket.

Women’s Yumiori Off Peak Full Zip Jacket.

During the summer months, it’s all about the mani-pedi. But once that icy weather blows in, self-care starts to look a bit different. The North Face’s Etip Gloves are basically a hand treatment on the go. Crafted from soft, stretchy fleece made with 93% recycled polyester, these tech-friendly gloves will keep your hands comfortable on cold-weather outings. They’ll also keep you connected: Touchscreen compatibility lets you check your phone without taking them off, while silicone grip dots on the palms help you hold onto your device as well as smaller essentials like keys and credit cards.

According to recent reports, for footwear, the Women’s THERMOBALL Traction Mule V will promptly become the standout of your seasonal lineup. These cloud-like slip-ons pair warm insulation with a quilted upper that gives them a casual, streetwear-cool vibe. The rubber outsole adds traction for quick trips outdoors.

Women’s THERMOBALL Traction Mule V.

Recent findings suggest that the minimalist philosophy requires you to take off one item before leaving the house. But during the cold weather season, it’s in your best interest to do the opposite. As you walk out the door, make sure you grab a beanie since most of your body heat can escape from your head.

It has been revealed that beanies are simultaneously the most underappreciated outfit addition and the most indispensable. The North Face’s Wool Blend Beanie, for instance, pairs the warmth of its 65% merino wool knit with a refined, metropolitan style. Its classic cuffed design and textured knit add visual interest, while its deep fit offers roomier coverage. If you prefer the rectangular logo with the same cuffed look, you can never go wrong with the rib-knit and soft lining of the Salty Lined Beanie. On the slopes or on your morning commute, either will add a polished finishing touch.

The importance of a functional winter hat cannot be overstated—think of it as the final brushstroke in the art of winter layering.

#146166. Industry News: China’s Luxury Problem Is Bigger Than the Economy

Industry News: China’s Luxury Problem Is Bigger Than the Economy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • China’s luxury slowdown is proving harder to reverse than many of the industry’s biggest players had hoped.
  • Recent findings suggest that after tentative signs of recovery, LVMH’s Fashion and Leather Goods division saw organic sales decline 5% in the third quarter of 2026, reversing a brief return to growth in the previous quarter (+1%).
  • It has been revealed that china’s property downturn, weak consumer confidence and uncertainty over future incomes help explain the sluggish demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China’s luxury slowdown is proving harder to reverse than many of the industry’s biggest players had hoped.

Recent findings suggest that after tentative signs of recovery, LVMH’s Fashion and Leather Goods division saw organic sales decline 5% in the third quarter of 2026, reversing a brief return to growth in the previous quarter (+1%). Gucci’s comparable sales fell 6%, weighed down partly by weak mainland Chinese traffic, while Prada Group also reported subdued footfall in the market. Even Richemont, whose jewelry houses have been among the industry’s most resilient performers, reported soft demand in mainland China, despite delivering 17% group sales growth at constant exchange rates in the six months to September.

It has been revealed that china’s property downturn, weak consumer confidence and uncertainty over future incomes help explain the sluggish demand. But experts agree the industry’s challenges run deeper than the economic landscape. Chinese consumers are reassessing what luxury is worth — and whether the brands that once defined aspiration still deserve their custom.

Sources indicate that “The spending capacity of affluent Chinese consumers remains intact; the criteria by which value is judged have changed,” says Wenbo Li, partner and Greater China regional lead at strategy and pricing consultancy Simon-Kucher, in response to official figures that suggest China’s luxury slowdown is unfolding against a more complex consumer backdrop. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, per capita disposable income rose 4.4% in real terms during the first nine months of 2026, while total retail sales reached RMB 41.6 trillion ($6.2 trillion) in the first 10 months, up a modest 1% year-on-year. More tellingly, retail sales of services grew 4.9%, far outpacing the 0.9% increase in goods sales.

After tentative signs of recovery, LVMH’s Fashion and Leather Goods division saw organic sales decline 5% in the third quarter.

Recent findings suggest that for luxury houses accustomed to commanding a premium through heritage, exclusivity and brand recognition, the implications extend beyond weaker sales. From dissatisfaction with customer service at luxury boutiques to rising expectations for meaningful experiences and renewed appreciation of domestic craftsmanship, Chinese shoppers are increasingly willing to question the value luxury brands claim to offer.

For Western luxury executives, understanding China’s slowdown cannot neglect a more uncomfortable question: What happens when consumers no longer need Western luxury brands to tell them what is desirable?

Industry observers note that for much of China’s luxury boom, exclusivity was not a barrier to consumption. It was the point. Luxury houses cultivated scarcity, controlled access and raised prices, making ownership a marker of social distinction. For aspirational Chinese consumers, gaining entry into this exclusive world was part of the appeal. The unwritten rules were widely accepted, which is the more one spent, the greater the access and recognition one could expect. But Chinese consumers are increasingly questioning those rules, particularly the expectation that respect and attentive service must be earned through spending.

Industry observers note that on Xiaohongshu, an increasing number of shoppers have shared complaints about dismissive treatment in luxury boutiques, especially when sales associates perceive them as unlikely to make a purchase. In November, Chinese fashion designer Lan Yu publicly criticized the attitude of Western luxury houses in a video referencing a leading luxury brand following an earlier account of an unpleasant boutique experience. The video attracted more than five million views, 31,000 likes and over 2,800 comments, with many owners sharing similar experiences of feeling judged or unwelcome in luxury stores. The response suggests that frustration with the power imbalance between brands and customers extends well beyond isolated encounters.

Recent findings suggest that yann Bozec, co-founder and managing director of consultancy YB Stratis and former president of Tapestry Asia-Pacific, questions the industry’s reliance on exclusion to create demand. “Exclusivity, by definition, means excluding people. I question whether making consumers feel excluded is a healthy or sustainable way to create desire,” he says.

According to recent reports, the tension became particularly visible in late September, when Tiffany & Co. faced a social media backlash after a customer in Chengdu complained on Xiaohongshu that a Mid-Autumn Festival mooncake gift had been sent to another high-spending client, but they hadn’t received it. The customer, who claimed to have spent more than RMB 200,000 ($30,000) at Tiffany, was dissatisfied with the brand’s response. Their post went viral, and in the days that followed, multiple related discussions around luxury customer service reached Weibo’s trending lists, prompting wider debate about preferential treatment, customer entitlement and the relationship between luxury spending and recognition. Tiffany apologized and confirmed improvements to its service procedures.

What has changed is that consumers are increasingly willing to publicly challenge this system built around customer hierarchies, rather than accept it as the price of entering luxury’s world.

The disconnect is also reflected in research. Simon-Kucher’s 2025 Luxury Consumer Study found that 36% of Chinese respondents were dissatisfied with personalization, 31% with communication frequency and 30% with customer engagement effectiveness.

“The biggest disconnect is not necessarily price itself, but the gap between what luxury brands offer and what Chinese consumers perceive as valuable, particularly in terms of personalization, relevance and customer engagement,” says Wenbo Li.

Luxury brands still need exclusivity to sustain desirability. But increasingly, Chinese consumers are drawing a distinction between exclusive products and exclusionary treatment. The former may justify a premium, but the latter risks driving them away.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge extends beyond how luxury brands make Chinese consumers feel about themselves. It is also about what consumers actually get in return for their spending. Today, a designer handbag no longer competes only with another handbag, but also with travel, fine dining, wellness, and cultural experiences that offer alternative forms of enjoyment and fulfillment.

It has been revealed that “Consumers aren’t necessarily spending less. Having already experienced most of the material side of life, they are no longer paying simply for the end-product, but are more discerning about the experience journey,” claims Vera Wu, director and head of commercial property, Westbund Central (a Hongkong Land property).

Recent findings suggest that simon-Kucher’s research found that more than two-thirds of surveyed Chinese consumers view luxury as a lifestyle encompassing purchases, experiences and ways of living. For luxury houses and the retail destinations that accommodate them, the implications of this are increasingly tangible. A prestigious brand name may still attract affluent customers, but it does not necessarily give them a compelling reason to return.

Sources indicate that hongkong Land’s Westbund Central in Shanghai offers one example of how luxury retail operators are responding. The RMB 60 billion ($9 billion) mixed-use development, with a planned gross floor area of approximately 1.7 million square meters, brings together retail, dining, wellness, cultural programming and public spaces.

Westbund Central’s opening program included a mindfulness session led by Jesse Israel in collaboration with Lululemon.

Its opening initiatives have included outdoor artistic performances, an installation by British artist Morag Myerscough and a mindfulness session led by Jesse Israel in collaboration with Lululemon. Rather than positioning shopping as the sole attraction, the development seeks to give consumers reasons to spend time in the space, even without an immediate intention to buy.

Recent findings suggest that “What is emerging is a demand for knowledge, and for a journey that feels both unique and refined,” says Wu. “We aren’t filling a mall in a single quarter; we are cultivating a neighborhood over a decade.”.

Perhaps the biggest challenge to luxury’s recovery in China lies in a more fundamental shift: Chinese consumers are beginning to question the definition of luxury that European houses have long dominated.

For decades, Western luxury brands served as benchmarks for taste, quality and prestige. Their heritage and craftsmanship helped establish that authority, while global recognition gave their products a status that extended well beyond their physical qualities. But as Chinese consumers become more experienced and discerning, they increasingly question how much of the premium they pay reflects the product itself and how much rests on the power of the brand name.

“At some point, the brand became more key than the product. We created an industry where the label itself became the source of value, sometimes overshadowing the craftsmanship and creativity that made luxury desirable in the first place,” notes Bozec.

That critique carries particular weight in China, where a renewed appreciation of the country’s own artisanal heritage is challenging the assumption that exceptional craftsmanship and refinement must come with a European label. Long before European fashion houses became global symbols of refinement, China had developed sophisticated traditions of silk-making, jewelry and decorative craftsmanship. Today, these traditions are finding renewed relevance. Chinese designers, artisans and entrepreneurs are revisiting historical techniques and cultural references, bringing them into contemporary products, with great success.

According to recent reports, laopu Gold is among the most commercially successful examples of this approach. Drawing on traditional Chinese goldsmithing techniques and cultural motifs, the brand — launched in 2016 — has surged in recent years as Chinese consumers favor domestic players.

The brand reported a 60.3% increase in revenue to RMB 19.81 billion ($2.97 billion) in the first six months of the year, while net profit surged 88.2% to RMB 4.27 billion ($640.5 million). Its appeal also extends to consumers of international luxury brands. According to Frost & Sullivan research, Laopu Gold’s customer base had an average overlap of 82.4% with five leading luxury brands — Louis Vuitton, Hermès, Cartier, Bulgari and Tiffany — as of March 2026.

It has been revealed that laopu Gold’s success also points to a broader shift in China’s fashion and luxury landscape. A newly introduced generation of homegrown brands, such as Songmont, Pane and To Summer, is building its own aesthetic identity and attracting increasingly discerning domestic consumers without relying on Western creative directors, imported heritage, or international recognition to establish credibility. Rather than seeking validation from established European fashion capitals, these brands draw on Chinese craftsmanship, local cultural references, and a deeper understanding of domestic tastes to define desirability on their own terms.

In a recent development, shoppers queue outside a Laopu Gold store. The brand’s revenue rose 60.3% to RMB 19.81 billion in the first half of the year.

This is particularly relevant in China, where sophisticated manufacturing capabilities and greater access to domestic and international alternatives have broadened consumers’ understanding of quality and design. With more points of comparison, shoppers are increasingly confident in making their own judgments about what deserves a premium today, rather than relying on established brand reputations.

“What does this product mean to me? Does it reflect my own taste and sense of style, rather than simply the status of the brand?” Bozec asks, describing the questions he believes younger consumers are bringing to luxury purchases.

Simon-Kucher’s 2025 Luxury Consumer Study provides some evidence of this diversity in consumer motivations. Some 45% of Chinese respondents were classified as “Fashion Forward Icons”, who are more experimental with their purchases, compared with 15% in Europe and 11% in the US. Another 25% were identified as “Quiet Luxury Enthusiasts”, who prioritize craftsmanship and timelessness, while just 10% fell primarily into the “Status Shoppers” category.

The findings point to a market where consumers are seeking different forms of luxury value, from creative originality and personal style to exceptional craftsmanship and lasting quality.

Recent findings suggest that china’s luxury market is not short of consumers who can afford expensive products. Nor do the rise of domestic competitors and the growing appeal of experiences suggest that demand for luxury goods is disappearing. What is less certain is whether the strategies that fueled the industry’s previous expansion can deliver the same returns.

Simon-Kucher’s Li expects China’s luxury market to recover gradually, but warns that “the previous growth model built on continuous price increases and an expanding customer base is unlikely to return.”.

“Ultimately, restoring demand in China requires shifting from price-led premiumization to value-led differentiation,” he adds.

According to recent reports, that distinction carries different implications across the industry. For some houses, it will require renewed emphasis on product quality, creativity and craftsmanship. For others, the priority may be improving customer relationships or creating experiences that justify a premium beyond the product itself.

Bozec offers a broader perspective on what fashion should contribute to consumers’ lives.

It has been revealed that it is a different proposition from selling consumers a ready-made identity through brand recognition and social status. Brands should place greater emphasis on how the product or experience improves an individual’s life. “For me, fashion is one of the tools an individual has to express himself, and even more to discover himself,” Bozec notes.

Economic confidence will remain crucial to any sustained recovery in China’s luxury market. But an improvement in sales should not be mistaken for a restoration of the industry's previous relationship with Chinese consumers.

The generation that helped build China’s luxury boom has accumulated not only wealth, but experience, knowledge, and alternatives. Luxury houses still have the opportunity to shape their aspirations, but they can no longer take that influence for granted.

#146165. How Will Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Dress?
