How Will Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Dress?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when Terence Young, the director of Dr.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Connery’s suits were considered relatively contemporary, because Anthony always had a very soft shoulder on his suits,” explains Elliot Mason, the director of business at Anthony Sinclair, which is no longer located on Savile Row, but still makes classic British suiting.
  • Opting to dress James Bond in a Savile Row suit might seem like a no-brainer in hindsight, but the decision—and the cut of the suits themselves—still resonates more than 60 years later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when Terence Young, the director of Dr. No, needed a suit for Sean Connery to wear for his debut as James Bond, he took him to see his personal Savile Row tailor, Anthony Sinclair.

Recent findings suggest that “Connery’s suits were considered relatively contemporary, because Anthony always had a very soft shoulder on his suits,” explains Elliot Mason, the director of business at Anthony Sinclair, which is no longer located on Savile Row, but still makes classic British suiting. “Anthony liked to nip in the waist, so it gave that real hourglass silhouette to the suit, which really is quite timeless. And as was the trend at the time, the Connery suits all had a relatively high rise, double-pleated with English forward pleats, and most of his trousers had Daks button-tab adjusters on the side.”.

Opting to dress James Bond in a Savile Row suit might seem like a no-brainer in hindsight, but the decision—and the cut of the suits themselves—still resonates more than 60 years later. Sinclair would make all of Connery’s suits during his nine-year run as James Bond, and his blend of classic British tailoring and of-the-moment influences would create a template for every Bond to come. With Robert Pattinson—a Dior ambassador and a guy with a reputation for adventurous style—chosen to take up the mantle in Bond 26, the question now becomes: what will he wear?

Tailor Anthony Sinclair fitting Sean Connery for one of the suits he wore in 1963’s From Russia With Love.

Ian Fleming, the author who created James Bond, spent a lot of time talking about what Agent 007 drank (Wolfschmidt Vodka) what he drove (Bentley convertibles, for the most part) and how he made his coffee (he was a dedicated pour-over guy), but, surprisingly, he never specified where the spy bought his clothes. As a result, for the last six decades, it’s been up to the directors and costume designers of the 25 previous films to create a latest look for every successive Bond. In the Connery and Moore eras it was Savile Row suits. Timothy Dalton’s Bond wore Paul Smith. Brosnan was a bespoke Brioni guy, as was Daniel Craig, who also brought Tom Ford into the mix. At 6’1” to Craig’s 5’10”, with a leaner build, and a long track record of fashion-forward dressing, Pattinson has everything needed to reinvent Bond once again.

It has been revealed that “I’m pretty sure we’re going to see something quite different from Pattinson's Bond,” says Matt Spaiser, the tailoring obsessive behind BondSuits.com and the author of From Tailors with Love: An Evolution of Menswear Through the Bond Films. “Pattinson is a different kind of actor, and he’s going to wear something that moves differently. Plus, he’s 18 years younger than Daniel Craig.”.

The actor playing Bond has a major influence on how he dresses—Daniel Craig, an adventurous dresser himself, was very hands-on with the wardrobe in his films—but Pattinson’s ongoing contract with Dior could also factor in. “Some of his Dior looks look somewhat like James Bond—he wears a great tuxedo—but I don’t think it’s going to tell us what he’s going to wear as James Bond,” Spaiser indicates. “He’s worn suits from other brands in other roles—like in Tenet, he wasn’t wearing a Dior suit—so I don’t think he's necessarily obligated to be wearing Dior as James Bond.”.

Daniel Craig, seen here in 2019 with then-Prince Charles on the set of No Time to Die, mainly sported sharp Tom Ford suiting in his later Bond films.

Recent findings suggest that another important factor that contributes to a upcoming Bond’s look is what’s happening in fashion whenever the film eventually gets made. “One thing that we've seen throughout most of the Bond eras is that he dresses in suits that are fairly traditional, but there's always some nod to the era that they’re in,” says Spaiser. “Sometimes they lean a little more into fashion, like when Roger Moore was wearing flares. That was something that I think they couldn't avoid without making Bond look too old-fashioned at the time.”.

Tone also plays an important role, and historically has ping-ponged between serious (Connery, Dalton, Craig) and more campy (Moore, Brosnan), but with Denis Villeneuve, the auteur behind Sicario, Blade Runner: 2049, and Dune in the director’s chair, the smart money isn’t on hovercraft gondolas and punny Bond girl names. A darker, more atmospheric milieu could make for an interesting complement to Pattinson’s taste for high-fashion.

Recent findings suggest that if Mason were dressing Pattinson for the role, he says, he’d take a lead from his clientele, many of whom, like Bond, are well-heeled Londoners with a taste for expensive sports cars and well mixed cocktails. “The majority of our customers are reasonably conservative, and when it comes to fit, they’re sensitive to current trends,” Mason notes. As such, he’d opt for longer jackets, both single- and double-breasted, that are fuller through the body, and straight-leg pleated trousers. “It’s not that very, very slim fit that we'd seen for so many years, but it still needs to be refined,” he says. “I don’t think it would be appropriate to put him in wide-leg or baggy trousers. I just don't think it’s right for Bond.”.

Robert Pattinson, the latest 007, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for over a decade.

Given the intense scrutiny on every relaunch of the Bond franchise, and the tendency of fans to get worked up online over perceived mishandling of a beloved character, Pattinson, Villeneuve, and the film’s yet-to-be-announced costume designers have little room for error. Go too conservative and they’ll be accused of playing it safe; make Bond into a fashion guy, and they’ll incur the wrath of the traditionalists.

“He needs to look current, but also timeless,” Spaiser indicates. “It’s a hard balance to find.”.

Taylor Swift has been spotted at all of Travis Kelce’s home games this season, and today’s matchup against the Arizona Cardinals was no exception. The singer was photographed with her parents, Andrea and Scott Swift, as she cheered on the Kansas City Chiefs. She wore a red and black jacket.

Recent findings suggest that swift has been out of the public eye since Wednesday, when she performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years. She attended the ceremony with Kelce’s teammate Patrick Mahomes’s wife, Brittany Mahomes.

Neither Kelce nor Patrick was with them at the ceremony, as the two NFL players are in the middle of their season.

Kelce has also been recovering from an ankle injury that sidelined him for part of the Chiefs’ game against the Atlanta Falcons last Sunday.

Recent findings suggest that after the game, he told USA Today that he was doing fine. “I’m all good,” he stated. “I probably could have done more than I did when I came back, but it was the direction the team wanted to go, so I was right there with them. We had a lot of young guys step up, so it was really nice.”.

In March, the 37-year-old tight end spoke on The Pat McAfee Show about how Swift inspired him to play another season.

According to recent reports, he mentioned that “without a doubt [watching her be on top of her field motivated me to continue playing]. We share the same love for what we do and fortunately, we’ve had this desire since we were kids in our selective professions.”.

“It’s just amazing to see her keep going to the table,” he noted of her music career. “Keep finding new things to write about. Keep finding new melodies and things like that. And on top of that, still seeing her have that love and joy in what she does, of course that’s motivating. That’s motivating for anyone to see, let alone you know, [me watching] my fiancée and knowing that I’m going through something where I’m trying to figure out exactly what the future holds for me. Something like that definitely motivates me to say, ‘You know what? I’m not done either. I’ve still got some ideas in the back of my mind. I’ve still got some juice left to play this game.’”.

The Newly introduced Rules for Selling Beauty in China

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that since Yang Zifeng and Zhou Tiancheng rolled out Flower Knows in 2016, the Chinese beauty brand has captured the local market with its ultra-feminine, fairytale-inspired aesthetic.
  • This May marked a new chapter for Flower Knows, which sold a majority stake to Proya Cosmetics as part of a RMB 351 million (roughly $52.6 million) deal — a move that reflects how far C-beauty has come, for both the acquired and the acquirer.
  • Industry observers note that founded in 2003, Proya began as a single skincare brand, offering proven active ingredients at accessible prices to China’s lower-tier cities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that since Yang Zifeng and Zhou Tiancheng rolled out Flower Knows in 2016, the Chinese beauty brand has captured the local market with its ultra-feminine, fairytale-inspired aesthetic. Think whimsical collections of lip glosses, blushes, and eye palettes that favor softer, buildable colors and sheerer applications, drawing on the duo’s passion for cosplay — for which they have built a sizable following in China under the stage names Baozi and Hana.

This May marked a new chapter for Flower Knows, which sold a majority stake to Proya Cosmetics as part of a RMB 351 million (roughly $52.6 million) deal — a move that reflects how far C-beauty has come, for both the acquired and the acquirer.

Industry observers note that founded in 2003, Proya began as a single skincare brand, offering proven active ingredients at accessible prices to China’s lower-tier cities. It expanded into a multi-brand group in the late 2010s – anchored by its 2017 IPO listing and 2019 acquisition of the Chinese makeup brand Timage. In 2024, Proya surpassed RMB 10 billion ($1 billion) in annual revenue, making it China’s largest beauty company.

It has been revealed that proya’s decision to acquire Flower Knows highlights its strategy to buy rather than build, as it diversifies beyond its flagship skincare brand of the same name. The group first invested in Flower Knows last August and, in May, acquired an additional stake, raising its total ownership to 51%. The move is part of Proya’s ambitious plan to become one of the top 10 global cosmetics companies by 2035, with a target of RMB 50 billion ($7.5 billion) in annual revenue. Proya’s stock jumped 5.1% on the Shanghai Stock Exchange following the announcement.

Yang Zifeng and Zhou Tiancheng rolled out Flower Knows in 2016.

Proya’s aim represents a bigger shift for the market. China’s beauty landscape over the past decade has evolved from low-cost dupes of Western and Korean cosmetics into a value-driven, culturally distinct global powerhouse capable of commanding serious valuations. Now, having secured majority market share at home, many C-beauty brands are setting their sights on overseas expansion and are moving past social media buzz into controlled offline retail channels to build long-term profitability and trust.

“Over the past decade, we’ve built a distinct creative identity and a passionate community. At the same time, we recognize that the beauty market is becoming more competitive and consumers are more selective about where they spend,” claims Flower Knows’s global CMO Fang Gongyiliu. “That makes it even more important to invest in product innovation, operational efficiency, and sustainable brand building, rather than relying on short-term trends. Our ambition isn’t simply to become a bigger brand, but to become a more enduring one.”.

Industry observers note that china is the world’s second‐largest consumer market for cosmetics. The latest data from the National Bureau of Statistics of China shows that cosmetics retail sales in September 2026 generated RMB 39 billion ($5.85 billion), up 5.4% year-on-year. Meanwhile, cosmetic retail sales in the country between January and September 2026 totaled RMB 349 billion ($20.9 billion), up 6.1% compared to the same period in 2025.

Driving the sector are multinational legacy brands, such as Chanel Beauty, La Mer and L’Oréal (the group’s business in mainland China returned to growth in late 2025 and continued its momentum into 2026), and rapidly surging domestic players, like Proya, Florasis and Maogeping, which collectively command more than half the domestic market, according to the China Association of Fragrance, Flavor and Cosmetic Industries.

Hua Mantian and Freeman Ren co-launched Florasis, selling cosmetics infused with traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) concepts and local craftsmanship and aesthetics.

It has been revealed that and while K-beauty has taken the world by storm, surpassing the US to become the second-largest beauty exporter globally, Chinese consumers have generally shown little interest. It’s in part due to historical geopolitical tensions that resulted in unofficial restrictions starting in 2016 on South Korean cultural and consumer goods. K-beauty’s market share in China has fallen sharply from 66% to 20%, according to 2025 Euromonitor data. In recent years, Korean beauty conglomerate Amorepacific reported that its North American business had overtaken its China revenue.

Recent findings suggest that china operates as a self-contained ecosystem distinct from Western or other Asian markets. In the latter, shoppers tend to rely heavily on physical stores like Sephora or Olive Young for product discovery and hands-on testing. China’s retail ecosystem, on the other hand, is built around native, digitally integrated super-apps, such as Baidu (China’s dominant search engine), Douyin and Xiaohongshu (which play a central role in brand discovery and reviews); transaction hubs like Taobao, Tmall, JD.com and even discount site Pinduoduo; and WeChat and Alipay (which combine messaging and mobile payments, as cash and traditional credit cards are rarely used).

“The Chinese consumer is probably not seeing all these ads on Medicube or the other dozen beauty brands that are doing very well globally,” indicates Cherrie Rao, a former marketing executive who recently relocated to the US after living in Beijing and Shanghai for the past decade.

Thus, local visibility is crucial. That’s why most C-beauty players start online. In 2017, when Hua Mantian and Freeman Ren co-launched Florasis, selling cosmetics infused with traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) concepts and local craftsmanship and aesthetics, they bypassed traditional brick-and-mortar retail, focusing primarily on DTC distribution via local platforms like Tmall. Flower Knows has also sold primarily through digital platforms like Taobao, where it frequently hosts livestream broadcasts and ranks among top category sellers. But reaching Chinese consumers requires more than just local platform integration.

Sources indicate that “Over the past decade, we’ve learned that storytelling alone isn’t enough to build a lasting beauty brand,” says Flower Knows’s Fang. “We often say that our products are the most crucial form of content. The intricate packaging, colors, textures, and the experience of opening a product give our consumers something worth discovering and sharing… But how it performs and how it fits into their everyday routine is what helps turn that interest into a purchase.”.

Florasis’s key is connecting with consumers beyond recognizable aesthetics. “‘Eastern elegance’ is more than a visual style. It represents a contemporary way of living”, a spokesperson tells Vogue Business. Indeed, while consumers in China are not a monolith and span vastly different regions and thus experiences and preferences, they share a cultural foundation — including an extraordinarily rich tradition of proverbs and idioms — that continues to deeply shape people’s moral values, social behavior and daily choices.

In a recent development, “I think the companies who are [driving] cultural confidence are the ones who are truly living the philosophy behind Chinese culture as well,” says Jess Tang, the founder of Dumpling, an Asia-focused brand strategy and design practice, and former head of Asia insights at forecasting firm WGSN. In C-beauty, this requires a real commitment to the community, she explains. “They’re building a business that is not just about making money, but is giving back to their country, to their hometown, to the villagers.”.

In a recent development, chinese fragrance houses like To Summer and Documents have built entire sensory worlds around cultural traditions and objects. Since launching in Beijing in 2018, To Summer has worked directly with local farmers to extract native botanicals like Jingmai Pu’er tea, Hubei osmanthus and Xinhui tangerine peel. Its retail spaces are often set inside restored historic courtyards and heritage buildings featuring Jingdezhen porcelain and traditional craft. Founded in Shanghai in 2021, Documents reinterprets not only traditional incense but also historical Chinese scent-wearing traditions, using knotted bag charms for its 5ml perfumes (instead of standard spray bottles).

Meanwhile, the C-beauty brand Maogeping Cosmetics has become a national success story since its launch in 2000 by the namesake makeup artist. Widely celebrated as China’s first homegrown luxury beauty brand, Maogeping broke a decades-long monopoly held by Western and Japanese cosmetics giants in China’s high-end department stores and culminated its 24-year rise with a landmark HK$2.3 billion (about $300 million) IPO in Hong Kong in December 2024, turning its founder into a billionaire. Strong momentum has continued following its listing, with the firm reporting 2025 full-year revenues of RMB 5.1 billion ($757 million), up 30% year-over-year.

According to recent reports, at the heart of Maogeping’s approach is education. While most beauty brands in China prioritize e-commerce, Mao invested in hundreds of department store counters across China, using these sites not simply as points of sale but as beauty studios where trained consultants offered personalized makeup lessons and demonstrations. The company also runs its own school, teaching makeup artistry, styling, and image design, across 11 cities in China, including Beijing, Hangzhou, Chongqing and Wuhan. In Tang’s view, this contributes to the local ecosystem. “I find that powerful because, from an Asian perspective, you have to give back as much in order to grow.”.

Riding the wave of cultural pride — dubbed the “guochao” movement, where Chinese millennials and Gen Z actively support domestic brands — has helped C-beauty brands to bypass the slower growth typical of upcoming companies.

In a recent development, but beyond growing national confidence, there has also been a major leap in the quality, design and innovation of C-beauty products over the past decade. Western or Korean brands simply “cannot keep up”, says Linda Yu, the general manager of Red Ant Asia, which advises global brands including Creed, Moncler, Charlotte Tilbury and Byredo on navigating China’s digital landscape and overseas retailers on which C-beauty labels to stock.

Rather than copying Western formulas, domestic companies such as Giant Biogene and Bloomage Biotech (which has backed Rao’s newly introduced brand, Alaris) invest heavily in proprietary R&D. Florasis, Flower Knows and Perfect Diary have turned packaging into collectible art. And brands including Judydoll (with its metal-wand “curling iron” mascara), Joocyee (for its high-performance lip formulas and jelly highlighters) and Winona (whose formulations are tailored to sensitive skin) have invented viral, functional products that Western competitors struggle to match.

Brands such as Joocyee, known for its high-performance lip formulas and jelly highlighters, have invented viral, functional products that Western competitors struggle to match.

Among C-beauty’s bright spots are color cosmetics, fragrance and beauty tools, of which online sales, tracked from January to September 2025, rose 5.4% to RMB 94.7 billion ($14.2 billion), compared to skincare, which remains the dominant category but fell 0.8% to RMB 207.8 billion ($31.2 billion), according to the latest data from Moojing, a Beijing-based consumer intelligence platform that tracks online sales across APAC.

However, amid China’s wider economic slowdown, “the overall guochao halo is fading,” warns Yu – not because Chinese consumers are returning to foreign brands, but because surface-level patriotism is no longer enough to sell a product. Thus, she says, “distinctiveness” remains key. Ellie Thorpe, director at intelligence firm Kantar BrandZ, agrees, noting that the strongest players in China compete on a point of view and give customers “a clear reason to choose them”.

Brands must also contend with changing beauty standards. While a fair, youthful and highly filtered look — coined by locals as 网红脸 wang hong lian, or “influencer face” — has long been the dominant beauty aesthetic, experts say this ideal is declining in favor of natural body types, healthy complexion and “no makeup” makeup. “I think beauty standards are becoming more diverse,” claims Rao, attributing the shift to the influx of K-pop and American culture on apps like Xiaohongshu. “There are now women who want to have sun-kissed skin or draw on freckles. They want to look healthy and natural.”.

Amid shifting consumer sentiment and intensifying local competition, domestic brands are also looking to offline retail channels, including overseas, for fresh pockets of growth. This indicates their ambition to compete on sustainable new customer acquisition and retention, rather than aggressive discounting via major local shopping events like Double 11 (also known as Singles’ Day), 520, Golden Week, and Qixi. Instead of chasing one-time bargain hunters, the focus now is on converting buyers into high-value repeat customers through prestige counters and mainstream retail partnerships.

From heritage festivals to digital shopping bonanzas, 2025 presents several opportunities to engage with China’s fast-changing market.

Florasis opened its first flagship in Hangzhou in 2022 and its first overseas store in Tokyo in 2025. Today, it is stocked by retailers in over 110 countries and regions, including Samaritaine Paris Pont Neuf in Paris, Skin Cupid in London, and Mall of the Emirates in Dubai. Meanwhile, Flower Knows expanded to Boots in the UK this March and physical Ulta stores in the US as of September. At home, it has entered specialty retailers such as Wow Colour (China’s answer to Sephora) and, in October, opened its first global flagship store on Huaihai Middle Road in Shanghai. China remains Flower Knows’s largest market overall, but the US has become its biggest internationally, Fang says.

Whether C-beauty can build lasting recognition outside of its home country remains to be seen.

But ultimately, the industry’s glow-up points to a bigger change, one where China is no longer a low-cost manufacturer and imitator, but a global powerhouse driven by original science, intricate design and innovation. See, for example, adjacent consumer industries like automobiles: China now leads the global EV industry, producing a majority of the world's electric cars and even collaborating with top European fashion figures like Kim Jones.

It has been revealed that “The idea is that the Chinese population should be creating things that are our own instead of mimicking trends in Korea or elsewhere, whether it’s politics or culture,” says Rao. “I see a shift where China has gone from being the world’s factory to becoming the world’s lab.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Sources indicate that toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

It has been revealed that add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It might seem strange, but it’s such an iconic flavor/texture combination.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chicken Francese is a staple at your favorite Italian restaurants. But sometimes, you don't want to empty your wallet for this classic dinner favorite. That's where I come in! Francese is a preparation (much like Milanese) that can be used with all types of meat and seafood, from shrimp to veal. For chicken, it involves dredging cutlets in flour and beaten egg, creating a pseudo-batter. The cutlets are then pan-fried and made crispy, albeit temporarily. See, chicken Francese is one of those dishes that epitomizes "crispy gone soggy"—a texture sensation that is one of my absolute favorites. In this case, the chicken becomes "soggy" because you finish them by simmering it in a rich, lemony sauce that will knock your socks off.

It might seem strange, but it’s such an iconic flavor/texture combination. Also, it is very easy to make and comes together in under an hour. What could be better?!

In a recent development, place 1 chicken breast on a cutting board. Using a sharp chef’s knife held parallel to the cutting board, slice into the thickest side of the breast, cutting three-quarters of the way through. Fold the top piece back (as if you were opening a book) and continue to cut until the breast is divided into 2 thinner cutlets. Repeat with the remaining chicken breast for a total of 4 cutlets. Working one piece at a time, place each cutlet between 2 sheets of plastic wrap. Using a meat mallet or the bottom of a small heavy skillet, pound the chicken to about 1/4" thick. Season all over with salt and pepper.

In a shallow dish, beat eggs, garlic powder, and a pinch of salt. Pour 1/2 cup flour into another shallow dish.

Industry observers note that in a large, heavy skillet over medium heat, heat oil. Working in batches, coat cutlets in flour, shaking off excess, then dip into the egg mixture, turning to coat.

Place cutlets in the oil, being careful not to overcrowd the skillet, and cook, turning halfway through, until golden brown, 5 to 7 minutes.

Transfer cutlets to a paper towel-lined plate to drain and season with salt and pepper.

Wipe out the skillet, then heat over medium heat. Add five Tbsp. butter and the remaining one Tbsp. flour, stirring until just beginning to foam and the butter is melted, 3 to 5 minutes. Whisk in wine. Increase heat to medium-high and bring to a boil. Cook, stirring, until slightly reduced, 1 to 2 minutes. Add stock, lemon zest, and lemon juice and return to a boil. Reduce heat to medium and cook, whisking constantly, until the sauce is reduced by about one-third, 3 to 5 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add lemon slices and remaining 1 Tbsp. butter and cook, stirring, until the sauce is glossy, 2 to 3 minutes more.

Return chicken to the sauce and cook, turning halfway through, until heated through, 2 to 3 minutes.

According to recent reports, transfer chicken to a platter and pour the sauce over. Top with lemon slices and parsley.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Sources indicate that if you have any leftovers, store them in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Luckily, this dish is used to being a tad soggy and lends itself well to being reheated in the microwave.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, surveying the best zip-up hoodies for men takes me back to my younger days as a hopelessly romantic high school kid. My formative years were marred by angst, soundtracked by pop punk, emo, and indie rock. The piece of clothing that got me through it all? A zip-up hoodie. It was core to the indie aesthetic, with every forlorn frontman sporting one over a thrashed band tee, skinny jeans, and shredded Chucks. But nostalgia never seems to stay in the past, especially when fashion is involved.

Industry observers note that gen-Z has revived every minute piece of 2000s pop culture, which means zip-up hoodies are back and have all but usurped the pullover hoodie as the sweat du jour. The zip-up is inherently versatile in both practical wear and sheer styling dexterity. With the flick of the zip, you can put your beloved Death Cab for Cutie tee on full display while letting your pits breathe, or keep it zipped up when it's just a bit too nippy out. To find the best zip-up hoodies on the market, I dusted off Transatlanticism and went on a deep dive. The good news is that the old classics are still good. The better news is that there's a lot of great competition to choose from.

Uniqlo’s no-nonsense clean aesthetic and low price point has made it a go-to for any menswear enjoyer looking for good style on a budget. While the brand excels at cashmere sweaters, T-shirts, and a slew of homerun collabs, the Japanese label’s sweats are criminally underrated. We’d go so far as to say that they should be talked in the same breath as brands like Champion and Sunspel. This zip up hoodie took us by surprise thanks to its comfy midweight, all-cotton fabric and solid construction. But the main selling point is the impeccable fit.

So many other brands cut their hoodies too long in the body and leave you looking like Jack Skellington’s pubescent brother. Uniqlo managed to cut its French terry hoodie to sit right at the hips which makes for a more classic and natural silhouette that’s neither lanky nor sloppy. Because of the fabric, the feel, and the overall fit, this is my favorite zip-up hoodie by a sizable margin. It’s my most-worn hoodie and has yet to show signs of any fraying.

Hoodies were originally meant for sportswear, as warm up gear before a grueling game of football. These days, they’re more often worn for lounging on the couch to watch the kickoff. And if you want to kick it in comfort while saving your pennies for booze and amuse bouche for the significant game with the boys, the best budget zip up hoodie to buy is Hanes’ EcoSmart zip hoodie. The fit is spot on—relaxed, but not sloppy, comfy in the body and the sleeves without swallowing you like a sand pit.

The fit is impressive for the price, and the overall quality means you’re getting a little more than what you pay for. It’s not a hoodie that’ll last you for too long, but it is a good quality piece for just 15 bucks. And when other hoodies offer lesser quality and worse-fitting options for about the same price? The answer is clear.

It’s hard not to sing the praises of Reigning Champ, a brand that built its fleece empire on sweatpants and hoodies. The Canadian label’s flagship midweight terry fabric has drawn the attention of streetwear royalty and menswear buffs alike and its dedication to quality has elevated the humble hoodie to oxygen-deprived heights. We named Reigning Champ’s crewneck sweatshirt and pullover hoodie as among our favorites in their respective categories, and the same goes for its zip-up hooded sweatshirt. It’s made of the same 100% cotton French terry fabric as its superlative-earning brethren and is cut with high-quality flatlock stitching for a smooth, un-bulky feel.

I had high expectations for Reigning Champ, given my previous experience, and I’m not surprised at all with how nice this zip-up is. And while I'm partial to the standard fit, it’s also available in a slim fit version, too.

In a recent development, hoodies live in a universe well beyond the sportswear world from which they originated. And while we still enjoy the OGs and the classics that made the hoodie a bona fide menswear must-have, we also love seeing all the ways the style has been pushed, tweaked, and freaked. Our Legacy's Level Hood has been a successful avenue for the Stockholm-based brand to explore the limits of the hoodie and this particular version strikes a delicate balance between the freaky and the fashion-curious. It's made of an English wool knit into an all-over ribbed texture for a throwback '90s feel. The cropped, boxy silhouette and elongated sleeves harken back to the grunge-y era, while the sultry dual-tone nightshade colorway throws you off in the best way possible.

According to recent reports, menswear influencers will be happy to regale you with their TedTalk on the golden ratio of clothing proportions. Essentially, that means your outfit should be divided into three equal sections where the top takes up one third of the outfit. Basically, your tops should be cropped and sit closer to your natural waist. Follow it up with some high-waisted pants with a wide silhouette and you’ve instantly garnered 300K views on TikTok (RIP). With so many indie brands and influencers scrambling to make their own versions of “the perfect cropped hoodie” you’re probably tired of wading through all the choices. Do yourself a favor and go to Abercrombie.

The Moose’s version is backed by actual trend forecasters, actual designers, and actual fit models. What does that mean, exactly? It means that its cropped zip hoodie fits really well and uses surprisingly beefy fabric. It was a revelation for me, too—Abercrombie wasn’t a name I associated with hoodies, but after I saw this in person, I had to readjust my menswear word cloud.

Some of the best zip-up hoodies for men are made by a brand you never see in brick and mortar stores. Camber has been crafting the most durable sweats for decades, right here in America and have been the shining example of the difference between good quality and great quality. Sure, you have to order through an old-school web 1.0 website and wait for several weeks to actually get your hoodie. But trust us when we say that the relatively minor inconvenience is completely worth it.

The heavyweight fleece is almost as thick as a leather jacket and can stand in as outerwear if you wanted it to. While other hoodies are washed to hell in giant industrial washing machines to reach a super soft texture by the time it gets to you, Camber’s actually require you to do the work yourself. It sort of feels like you’re being swaddled by an anaconda, which means if you’re a proponent of hard clothes like raw denim, you’ll like Camber’s hoodie a lot.

Recent findings suggest that cashmere zip hoodies, once the exclusive province of Silicon Valley unicorn founders and PJ-flying nepo babies, have been democratized, none better than Naadam's take. You know the brand for bringing thoughtful, sustainable cashmere pieces at “really, only that much?” prices. Its zip hoodie is as soft as it gets, with extra credit points awarded for coming in a classic fit (too many cashmere hoodies err on the side of slim) and six colors, including this decidedly handsome olive. Wear it on weekends, work-from-home Fridays, and long flights—even if it's just Economy+.

Sources indicate that shoutout to brother in arms Louis Cheslaw, GQ Recs contributor, whose writing for the newsletter Magasin put us on to young brand Cease. From seed to sewing, it's beefy 20-ounce cotton is fully American-made. Assembling the fabric vertically means the hoodie will shorten up to a slightly cropped, oversized fit. Act fast if you want some of the less-boring colors—they move fast.

Industry observers note that we can’t deny Russell Athletic’s contributions to the hoodie space. And while its formula has changed over the years, the newly introduced hoodies are still pretty good for the price. The fabric is soft and lightweight, and it’s available in a rainbow of colorways. Plus, if you’re looking for a hoodie with a little more length, this is a great option.

In a recent development, bold graphics aren’t usually deemed classics, but Gap’s retro-leaning collegiate-style block logo has staying power almost as much as the Levi’s red tab. Add to that a wonderfully fluffy midweight fleece material and a tailored straight fit and you’ve got something you’ll see on moodboards for generations to come.

According to recent reports, champion’s Reverse Weave fabric is iconic for its nearly shrink-proof quality and almost unsettlingly rough exterior. Flip it to the inside and you’ve got a luxuriously brushed interior that’ll have you feeling like you’re melting into a cloud. Heads-up that pricing varies kinda wildly by size on Amazon.

The secondhand market is chock full of navy-blue hoodies that have been sun-faded and beaten down with time. They'll cost you just as much as this Mfpen version, but will also fall apart faster than you can zip 'em up.

Industry observers note that les Tien's dedication to all things sweats results in a catalog of luxurious fleece and terry cloth with a modern approach. Featuring high-end Cobrax hardware, RiRi zippers, raw-edge hems and sleeves, and a heavyweight brushed fleece, no detail is phoned in.

Recent findings suggest that the Real McCoy's is considered by many to be Americana repro wizards. This revival of an early 20th-Century hoodie is just one small piece of the brand's preservation prowess. It's made using beefy sinker-knit fleece, old-school Talon-style zippers, and vertical patch pockets.

Industry observers note that A.Presse's chokehold on the menswear illuminati refuses to let up and it's pieces like this vintage-inspired hoodie that keep the pressure on. Based on very rare “after-hood parkas", this made-in-Japan hoodie features an idiosyncratic attached hood, super dense and lofty fleece, with artfully distressed details throughout.

Think of the zip-up as the pullover hoodie's elder brother, but with way more layering potential. In its most natural state, it can cuddle up to a matching set of sweatpants and a baggy tee with flair. (Top it off with a swanky necklace, crisp sneakers, and some stellar shades and you’re left with a fit on par with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at his tunnel-trotting best.).

Industry observers note that unzipped and left open, it can also take on the role of a picture frame ready to display your sickest graphic tee—much like the cardigan, another treasure of 2000s fashion. Or make like a mid-Aughts garage band ironically donning corporate attire and wear your zip-up over a dress shirt and baggy tailored trousers, a high-minded fashion move with a jolt of kooky Scandinavian cool.

In a recent development, style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Sources indicate that across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally fresh to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Sources indicate that whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.).

Breaking: Who Will Win the Chinese Sportswear Race?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Birding, surfing, camping, hiking, paddleboarding, basketball, yoga, weightlifting… in 2026, the demand for physical and outdoor activities is booming in China, and the country’s sportswear market is growing to meet it.
  • China’s sportswear market is worth $66.7 billion, according to Euromonitor, and is expected to reach over $73 billion by 2028.
  • “The sportswear market in China is moving from volume to specialization, led by growing demand for technical outdoor products, trail-running footwear and activity-specific apparel,” says Marguerite Le Rolland, Euromonitor’s head of footwear and apparel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Birding, surfing, camping, hiking, paddleboarding, basketball, yoga, weightlifting… in 2026, the demand for physical and outdoor activities is booming in China, and the country’s sportswear market is growing to meet it.

China’s sportswear market is worth $66.7 billion, according to Euromonitor, and is expected to reach over $73 billion by 2028. Though still dwarfed by the US sportswear market, which right now sits at $168 billion, China’s market is growing faster. As local consumers become more active and health-conscious, brands are expanding in what is fast becoming a large and increasingly diversified landscape.

“The sportswear market in China is moving from volume to specialization, led by growing demand for technical outdoor products, trail-running footwear and activity-specific apparel,” says Marguerite Le Rolland, Euromonitor’s head of footwear and apparel. “At the same time, Chinese companies are making the transition from manufacturing for global brands to building global brands of their own.”.

The rise in physical activity — helped along by the government’s Healthy China 2030 initiative, a major strategy rolled out in 2016 — is also having a knock-on effect on what people want to wear. “Overall, there’s a shift in status-signaling in China, from the upcoming-money major logo look, to the old money hobby and lifestyle-driven status,” states Allison Malmsten, China strategy consultant at Daxue. “As a result, we see white-collar office workers now sporting Arc’teryx and Descente to the office, rather than a luxury logo.”.

Sources indicate that while China’s sportswear market is ripe with opportunity, some Western megabrands are facing headwinds amid more selective consumer sentiment and a boom in domestic players. Nike’s Greater China business has suffered, with Q1 2027 revenue falling 26% in the region, while.

It has been revealed that china was a growth engine for Lululemon post-pandemic, but revenues in the region fell 2% in the second quarter of fiscal 2026. Adidas, after some difficult years in the region, is staging a recovery, with Greater China sales up 15% in the first nine months of the year. Meanwhile, more nimble local brands like Anta Sports are building multi-brand portfolios that are quickly gaining market share, with HSBC analysts calling Anta a “clear winner” over Nike for its higher profit margins in a recent research report shared with Vogue Business.

Sources indicate that the first Anta Market fashion sports concept store in Shanghai. According to HSBC analysts, Anta is a “clear winner” over Nike for its higher profit margins in a recent research report.

The tension between legacy incumbents and newer players is playing out in an increasingly fragmented market. The age of the general fitness buyer in China is over, and a more segmented landscape has emerged. “Five years ago, the market was driven by basic, all-purpose gear,” claims Eva Zhang, project director of ISPO China, a leading sportswear trade fair. “Today, niche tracks like trail running, lightweight hiking, and even pet outdoor gear are booming.” Some Western labels are benefiting from the shift: outdoor label Arc’teryx’s parent organization, Amer Sports, saw 30.4% growth in Greater China for Q3 2026.

ISPO’s Brand Showcase in Beijing in January 2027 aims to bring “international buyers closer to Chinese innovation,” notes Zhang.

It has been revealed that “Consumers have become far more knowledgeable and sophisticated about product function, materials and technical details,” adds Running Xie, general manager of insight, ideas and increment at Buy Promptly, a leading omnichannel e-commerce platform. “They demand category-specific technical gear, not one-size-fits-all athletic apparel.”.

Industry observers note that as less agile, more generalized incumbents struggle to adapt, local brands are stepping in to meet demand. Kailas, which specializes in trail running gear, is forecasting $1.7 billion in revenue this year. Xie points to major local brand Mobi Garden (camping gear), and mid-sized or smaller independent designer brands like UTO (known for fashionable base layers) and Tajezzo (functional backpacks), as just a few examples of names that have cornered a niche. They satisfy demand for sport-specific, professional-grade performance wear, which — even when it’s casual — helps telegraph knowledge, participation and status.

“Even if they don’t do it in a professional way, they need to have the professional item,” says Sophia Dumenil, co-founder of The Chinese Pulse. “It’s cooler to have the total look. It’s also a way to show that you take care of yourself. The new beauty standard [for women] that’s emerging is not about being delicate; it’s about being fit and healthy.”.

According to recent reports, at the same time, consumers also want sportswear they can wear when they’re not doing sports. Feng Chen Wang, who works with Under Armour on ‘Rebel Daughter’, a line of China-inspired sporty casualwear, has observed a blurring of boundaries between sportswear and everyday clothing in China — especially among Gen Z. “Sport isn’t a slot in the day; it lives inside the day,” notes the designer. “To reach a younger consumer, the garment has to be something you can wear into your life first.”.

Feng Chen Wang and Under Armour’s collaboration ‘Rebel Daughter’ is a line of China-inspired sporty casualwear.

The designer has focused on creating garments that aren’t built for competition but “light movement” — sporty-looking tracksuits with a contemporary fashion edge. “Young people’s lives now are looser, more varied, and they want convenience. Nobody needs to change three or five outfits a day,” she says. “The lines between occasion, function and fashion are being folded into one.”.

Industry observers note that beneunder, a brand that makes sun-protective clothing, highlights the potential of the shift. “Sun protection has evolved beyond a seasonal beauty concern into a broader lifestyle category,” notes Cindy Gong, Beneunder’s affiliate marketing manager. “Consumers increasingly want products that combine protection with comfort, breathability, lightweight design, and style. We believe this reflects a wider shift toward functional clothing that can transition naturally between everyday life and outdoor activities.”.

Beneunder, which makes sun-protective clothing, sees sun protection becoming “a broader lifestyle category” rather than a seasonal beauty concern, indicates affiliate marketing manager Cindy Gong.

As sportswear branches out into these various specialties, consumer motivations can be separated into what strategists at forecasting agency WGSN think of as ‘Push’ (think competitive sports like trail running, tennis and Hyrox) and ‘Pause’ (more restorative activities like birding, fishing and paddleboarding that can help overworked people to decompress). “Right now, everything falls into those two camps,” says Alison Ho, APAC strategist at WGSN. “Chinese consumers are either chasing a personal best or chasing peace. The brands that win will know which one they’re selling to.”.

Industry observers note that local brands in China are gaining influence, but they must still compete with international names that are stepping up their strategies to capture the Chinese market. Following a successful online launch in August, Alo Yoga has laid out looks to open nine stores across Greater China, while Reebok has set a target to open up to 200 outlets in mainland China by 2029.

To successfully capture the market and connect with local consumers, cultural nuance is key. Juliette Duveau, who runs The Chinese Pulse with Dumenil, points to Adidas’s collaborations with local designers, including Shuting Qiu and Edison Chen, and Nike, which has incorporated traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) into multiple products and activations in the country, for instance, with the Jordan brand, which hosted a TCM-themed pop-up in Shanghai in partnership with BMX rider Nigel Sylvester. Nike also prepares to design and develop 50% of its Nike Sportswear and Jordan products sold in China locally by fiscal 2030, per Reuters. At a time when many international brands face heat in China for cultural missteps, this kind of hyper-localized approach cuts through. “Just collaborating with a name today is not enough. The concept needs to be super-matching with what you want to do,” says Duveau.

The Adidas Originals Neo-Chinese SS27 collection.

Sources indicate that these localized activations are just the surface and hint at a larger macro shift in supply chains, with more products designed in China rather than just manufactured there. Nike’s announcement of its 2030 manufacturing goals is meant to better integrate into the market. “It’s no longer just placing orders and OEM manufacturing, but moving towards co-creation and joint R&D,” notes ISPO’s Zhang. “China is transforming from the world’s factory into a global innovation engine.”.

It has been revealed that at the same time, international giants face a rising tide of Chinese brands making their own inroads. In 2026, NBA player Stephen Curry signed a 10-year partnership worth a reported $400 million with Li-Ning, with Curry’s first shoe for the brand slated for release in 2027. Anta, China’s largest sportswear company, which opened its first US flagship in California in February, is implementing a broad strategy of investing in international sportswear businesses. It recently became the largest shareholder in Puma and is also the largest shareholder of Amer Sports (which itself owns Salomon and Wilson alongside Arc’teryx). “It brings brands that are already established and reassuring in terms of their sports authenticity and innovation capabilities directly into their ecosystem,” claims Duveau. “It also helps them to build credibility and legitimacy, which maybe gives Anta leverage to make their own brand more premium in the future.”.

It has been revealed that gorpcore label Uppervoid sorts its gear by altitude and trip length. “It’s specialists versus generalists,” indicates Ho.

Recent findings suggest that zhang says that while Chinese brands have the hard power to compete globally, the challenges are clear. “The stereotype of Made in China takes time to break, and moving from what is cost-effective to what is value-driven is the core challenge,” she says. In January 2027, ISPO will hold a Brand Showcase in Beijing, with exhibitors spanning outdoor and snowsports to camping and general lifestyle. “Our aim is to help Chinese brands amplify their brand value globally while bringing international buyers closer to Chinese innovation,” says Zhang.

Sources indicate that while the big names battle for global relevance, some believe smaller brands will come to the fore. “The most exciting energy is often below Anta and Li-Ning,” says Ho. She points to Aonijie, the official hydration partner of the UTMB World Series (a trail running circuit), and a newly introduced wave of design-forward labels that take a granular approach. Uppervoid, a gorpcore label whose slogan is “In Nature We Trust”, sells mountaineering gear that is segmented by altitude, and trekking clothing filtered by how many days you plan to spend on the road.

“This is no longer China versus the West,” says Ho. “It’s specialists versus generalists.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Here’s what’s available this November—there are some treats you don’t want to miss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the holiday season is on the horizon, and Costco is celebrating with plenty of festive foods in every corner of the warehouse. Aside from the obligatory pumpkin pie, you can find party-approved appetizers, cozy bakery treats, and plenty of fall-forward snacks.

I spend all year keeping tabs on the latest and greatest products to hit Costco shelves. And as someone who writes about Costco for a living, I have a hot take: The food at the warehouse right now is the best it’s been all year.

Here’s what’s available this November—there are some treats you don’t want to miss.

The viral sensation has officially hit Costco. The Dot Cakes is a bakery on Long Island, New York, that exploded in popularity this summer thanks to its signature dessert: a single-serving cake in a cup covered in a generous layer of nonpareil sprinkles. Now, instead of waiting in long lines or trying to recreate it at home, Costco members can buy a six-pack of the real thing.

Each box includes both chocolate and vanilla cake, and both flavors are perfectly nostalgic. They taste like the best-ever birthday cake from your childhood, and the crunch of the sprinkles makes the experience even more fun.

It admittedly takes a lot for us to get excited about grapes—but these are worth the hype. Shine Muscat is a premium variety from Japan, famous for its large, sweet, seedless fruit. Many of the ones sold in the U.S. are imported from East Asia, including these Korean grapes now available at Costco.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve had the pleasure of trying the grapes in smoothie form at a Costco food court in Seoul, but the real thing is even better. Our editors couldn’t stop eating them and compared the flavor to a plum or lychee. And at $10.99, they’re a fun upgrade that costs only a bit more than standard table grapes.

In a recent development, want takeout flavors without takeout prices? Costco is now selling a noodle stir-fry kit that can feed the whole family for around $15. Each tray includes crispy breaded chicken pieces, yakisoba noodles, vegetables, and a sweet-and-savory sauce.

The meal is super easy to put together: Just crisp up the chicken in the oven or air fryer, then heat everything else in a pan. Costco is generous with the chicken and noodles, so the kit can provide at least four substantial servings. But if you need just one reason to add it to your cart, do it for the sauce. It’s just sweet enough with the slightest hint of spice.

Recent findings suggest that cabot Creamery has already combined its cheddar with popcorn, but this fall-forward version balances the sharp, salty flavor with a bit of sweetness. Each bag includes two types of popcorn: one seasoned with Cabot’s famous Seriously Sharp Cheddar and another with a maple syrup-flavored coating. Both are delicious on their own, but together? Magic happens.

According to recent reports, the salty-sweet combo really works here, reminding us of those large popcorn tins with three different compartments, except everything’s mixed together. Your holiday movie marathon needs a bag of this.

Recent findings suggest that fans of the Kirkland Signature peanut butter pretzels need to grab this sweet treat. Jif’s Snappers combine mini pretzels, the brand’s creamy peanut butter, and a drizzle of milk chocolate. We love that there’s a higher peanut butter-to-pretzel ratio than with Kirkland Signature's version (and the PB is much softer). This snack has everything: It’s salty, sweet, crunchy, creamy, and impossible to put down.

According to recent reports, step aside, Snap, Crackle, and Pop. The brand Cloud 9 has upgraded the cereal-based sweet with flavors inspired by mango sticky rice. Each bar combines puffed rice with dried mango, coconut milk, and shredded coconut. And the Delish team agrees: This is arguably the best snack Costco has sold all year. It’s loaded with mango, lightly sweet, and full of interesting textures. Buy a bag and thank us later.

In just a few years, Swedish candy went from an uncommon novelty to a permanent fixture in the candy aisle. Now, Costco carries a Rolling Pin variety pack that includes sour gummies and foam candy (a Swedish staple with a marshmallow-like texture).

This 30-ounce bag features a wide variety of chewy textures and fruity flavors. If you’re just now dipping your toes into the world of Swedish candy, this is a great (and affordable) way to start.

Need fall breakfast inspo? Look no further. The newest addition to the Costco bakery is this maple pecan coffee cake, which is loaded with cream cheese, pecans, and maple flavor. The cake is topped with a crumbly pecan butter streusel and drizzled with the same icing Costco uses on its danishes.

In a recent development, each coffee cake is $15, but it’s arguably worth much more given its sheer size. This thing is a behemoth—it’s tall and absolutely loaded with toppings. There’s also a thick layer of filling in the center that tastes nearly identical to pecan pie filling.

Baked brie is a party showstopper, and Costco now carries a kit with everything you need in one convenient package. Stonemill Kitchens’ kit includes puff pastry, a wheel of brie, chopped pecans, and caramel apple cranberry chutney. You’ll need to assemble it yourself before you throw it in the oven, but the instructions couldn’t be simpler. The puff pastry even comes with a sheet of parchment paper to protect your baking sheet!

It has been revealed that and the results are straight-up showstopping. The melty, creamy brie pairs perfectly with the pastry and toppings. The chutney, despite the caramel in the name, isn’t too sweet—it adds just the right amount of festive holiday flavor. It’s so good that News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas even did a happy dance after taking a bite.

Abercrombie & Fitch’s resurgence has been well documented, and the brand shows no signs of slowing down. Alongside its familiar mix of timeless staples, contemporary silhouettes, and archival-inspired pieces, Abercrombie has introduced YPB, or Your Personal Best: a dedicated line of performance apparel designed to bring the same considered approach to the gym as it does to the rest of your wardrobe.

Recent findings suggest that comprising everything from tees and tanks to shorts and jackets, YPB reflects Abercrombie’s ability to evolve while staying true to its heritage. The collection makes a convincing case for performance wear that goes beyond the usual sea of uninspired basics and head-to-toe Lycra. It’s also versatile enough to seamlessly move from a strenuous workout to the everyday wardrobe rotation. To put the collection through its paces, we’ve styled three looks that show just how far YPB can go.

I am a chronic overheater so my gym outfits always reveal a bit of skin. (It’s also a vanity thing so I can see my muscles at work when I’m getting after it.) This vintage-inspired muscle tank looks like some of the actual vintage tees that I’ve taken a pair of scissors to without a stranger’s set-in stains. I have a lot of hair that gets in my way so headwear is a must when working out. A bandana is a nice throwback to the classic bodybuilder era and unlike a hat, it does a better job at soaking up the sweat so it’s not dripping down my face.

In a recent development, the standout of this outfit is the shorts. Compression lined, they’re about as long as I’d go for shorts clocking in with a five-inch inseam. They have a discreet pocket in the liner to store my phone, and they're tight enough so my device doesn’t go flying out when I’m doing high knees. Plus, they’re stretchy enough for hitting depth on a squat without risking a NSFW tear between the cheeks.

In a recent development, I’ve come to learn that recovery days are not only a blessing but a necessity. But they don’t necessarily mean you have to waste away on the couch all day. My active recovery days involve a lot of walking, and that means my workout shorts make an appearance once again. I can’t deny their comfort factor, and it’s hard to beat a sweater-and-shorts combo, an outfit beloved by my favorite A-listers.

Recent findings suggest that the sweater was a quarter-zip with an elastic waistband for a more streamlined, tailored fit. And if I’m walking a little too briskly, the top easily comes off to reveal a staple graphic tee in my wardrobe.

Finally, I put on some pants! I don’t make it a habit to wear sweatpants out casually, but sometimes the weather calls for it. Hike ‘em up a bit and show off some crisp white socks, a style swerve I saw once and couldn’t help but copy.

Sources indicate that the staple of this outfit is the heavyweight jacket. Its water-resistant lining keeps me dry when the meteorologists get the forecast wrong, and it’s lined to keep me warm as the days get shorter and the nights get longer. The two-way zipper also allows for some extra mobility, and it won’t bunch up when I sit down like so many other parkas.

Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare.
  • More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.
  • Industry observers note that place 1–1¼ lb.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Industry observers note that place 1–1¼ lb. boneless Latest York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; promptly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.).

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.
