💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release.
  • Grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child.
  • Sources indicate that I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release. It’s the first new installment of the franchise since 2013; the one whose first trailer was released three years ago; the one that probably cost over a billion dollars to produce; the one set in a satirical, fictionalized south Florida; the one described in this very magazine as “the peak of entertainment.” During my first four hours with the game, I made a few hundred dollars doing odd jobs, performed several repairs on my swamp-front fixer-upper, knocked out a few sets of kettlebell swings on the deck, did favors for two friendly neighbors, and ran a mile to retrieve a freshly repainted car I left behind at a fishing spot just outside of town. I’m writing in vague terms not only to avoid spoiling the game’s plot but because, so far, it hasn’t been all that exciting. The absurd and hyperrealistic mundanity of its gameplay is, simply, astonishing, and more than I ever could have wanted from a franchise I’ve been playing for nearly a quarter of a century.

Grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child. I wasn’t even aware of their existence until learning of the franchise’s third entry, and the first in 3D. I discovered GTA in a hotel room in Wichita Falls, TX, a small city just a stone’s throw from Oklahoma, because a classmate named Zach (or Zack) risked damaging his PS2 by toting it along on a school trip. We were there for the annual Texas Thespian Festival, an opportunity for dramatically inclined teenagers to perform plays and musicals in front of strange kids from strange schools and compete for prizes that, like most awards, quickly lost meaning after they were bestowed. After attending the required main stage productions, many of which were watered down to their school-friendly “Junior” adaptations—Into the Woods without the second act deaths and darkness, Guys & Dolls with considerably less gambling—we returned to the nearby hotel where students slept three to a room and were told to behave. For several nights we took turns playing this impossibly violent and vulgar game, five or six of us huddled around the television parked on a dresser no one used. We stole cars, killed non-player characters with assault rifles, and even completed an occasional story mission, most of which required, well, stealing cars and killing non-player characters with assault rifles. We were actors, and wasn’t gaming just another form of performance?

Sources indicate that I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity. Before that moment, he was simply an intimidatingly charming and friendly older boy I knew best for playing Romeo in a production that our school’s theater director chose to set during the Vietnam War for reasons he was unable to articulate. (In that, my first stage role, I was cast as Juliet’s unnamed little brother, a role that doesn’t exist in the original text.) Of course I’d played video games before that weekend—Myst, Rollercoaster Tycoon and a Titanic-themed mystery were my favorites at that point—but never before had I experienced something so immersive or graphically impressive. It was loud and exciting, a simulation of real life at its most extreme and chaotic. When I got home, I knew the console–and GTA 3–had to be mine. My life, laser-focused on math homework and our theater director’s post-apocalyptic interpretation of Antigone, could have really used a thrill.

According to recent reports, I traded in my PlayStation, a Christmas gift from years earlier on which I played mostly rented or borrowed adventure games, and used money I’d saved from mowing lawns (my family’s own, and those of a few elderly neighbors), to pay the balance. The only game I wanted was GTA III, and it’s the only one I played for months. The novelty was the thing. There was a story, of course: some nameless protagonist with a chiseled, low-polygon face committing crimes and various acts of violence to achieve a goal of… staying alive? Perhaps that’s the goal of most games, maybe even the goal of life itself. I skipped cutscenes in favor of driving from one glowing cylindrical marker to the next, shooting police officers in the head and picking up sex workers who did unseen, noisy things to my character that made the stolen cars bounce up and down like a lowrider with hydraulics. I’d largely missed the groundbreaking graphics of the N64 era—having never played Zelda or Mario Kart or GoldenEye outside the bedrooms of childhood friends with bigger houses and never-ending supplies of soda in the fridge—which meant my first truly passionate dive into console gaming was filled with manic, gratuitous violence. The original PlayStation was for catching troublemaking monkeys in nets and flying around gentle landscapes as a purple dragon. The PS2, though, was for imagining a life of crime. That my parents allowed me to play these games at all still surprises me, but I suppose to them anything was better than me getting drunk at parties I knew were happening but was never invited to.

Industry observers note that by the time Grand Theft Auto: Vice City was released the following year, I had a part time job at a local AMC, so I bought the game with money earned selling popcorn and cleaning that same popcorn off the floor. Playing it was a reward for completing an essay on Ernest Hemingway or telling multiple moviegoers that we couldn’t give refunds simply because they “didn’t like” Men In Black 2. The game’s soundtrack introduced me to songs that still activate memories sitting cross-legged on the carpet of my bedroom, turning the volume down as low as I could to prevent my father from stepping inside and saying, gravely, “Am I going to have to turn that off?” To this day, I can’t hear Laura Branagin’s “Self Control” without conjuring Tommy Vercetti, the protagonist of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, driving a motorcycle down a sparsely populated road flanked by neon-lit palm trees. For months, I listened to more in-game radio than the local Top 40 station, unaware at the time that its curated period playlists would shape my musical appetite for the rest of my life.

The third installment of that PS2 trilogy, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, came out two years later, when I was a freshman in college. I was 18, adjusting to life in a fresh city, and trying desperately to make friends. The game was less a reward for hard work than a balm when I didn’t feel like socializing, a distraction from my countless first semester anxieties. By the time I completed its main story, life away from home had become normal. I had new friends, new obligations, new problems. I used my PS2 as a DVD player almost exclusively, watching several movies a week, all borrowed from Netflix (during its original red-envelope form) and the school library. By the time GTA 4 was released, I’d lost interest in gaming altogether. We were in a recession, and I was hellbent on keeping my very first real job. In fact, I didn’t play another Grand Theft Auto game until 2013, on a PS3 Slim (the console’s discounted, late-generation entry), weeks after my now-husband and I moved into our first apartment together. In the time since my last GTA experience, I’d come out of the closet, moved across the country, started a new career, adopted my first cat, and made an entirely new group of close friends. A franchise that was once a distraction from teenage malaise was now pure, unadulterated fun. Gone were the days of playing it at a low volume–I turned it all the way up, and didn’t skip cut scenes. I was there for the story as well as the spectacle.

13 years later, the longest ever interval between newly introduced installments, my relationship with gaming has evolved alongside the games themselves. It’s not enough to be distracted; being distracted is now our default state. Disturbances arise, whether seeking them or not: a text message in the middle of a terrible Peacock show; a news alert regarding a global calamity about which you can do nothing but panic; the jittering beeps of FaceTime call while reading a wonderful novel, or that mindless, habitual scroll through a feed that highlights videos meant to be seen but not remembered. Lately I’ve turned to gaming for total immersion, for sensations of genuine awe that might keep me from succumbing to the dopamine rush of my phone. I spent much of the summer replaying Kingdom Come Deliverance and its sequel, a pair of life simulators set in medieval Europe. In those games, every action has a consequence, and every success is hard-fought and requires patience.

After several hours in its impossibly dense world, GTA 6 seems to be encouraging a similar sense of duty. My real life is fine, often even good. It’s the kind of life I thought impossible when the franchise first entered my life nearly a quarter century ago. I’m not bowled over by the game because it’s better or even more fun than the life I live outside Vice City—there are gun-toting mass murderers in both, after all—but because it’s totally different. Even when you’re comfortable in your own life, isn’t it extraordinary to enter another? The games have always been about adults, and for adults. It says so right on the box. Since 2002, their goals have fundamentally remained the same: get a job, make money, stay alive. As a teenager, its simulated depravity was funny and exciting, with graphics and gameplay so vivid I could feel like a kid again. But now, at 40? With 20-plus years of GTA under my belt and a life 16-year-old me would find more unbelievable than the functionalities of the PS5 Pro? No game has ever made me feel older. What a privilege that is.

According to recent reports, mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Recent findings suggest that cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

It has been revealed that reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Industry observers note that using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Welcome to In Good Company, where we ring in the festive season with fashion-insider entertaining tips, expert etiquette advice, and the perfect editor-approved hostess gifts.

Holiday entertaining brings with it countless conundrums—from uninvited guests to the cousin who won’t put down their phone—for both hosts and guests. Agility is the key word; being able to elegantly pivot and respond to unexpected situations is what makes people feel comfortable and appreciated. Just in time for festive gatherings, ELLE spoke with Lizzie Post, author, co-president of the Emily Post Institute, and co-host of the Awesome Etiquette podcast, about all the things to keep in mind for a kind and gracious holiday. Read on for Post’s refreshingly down-to-earth tips.

No one can keep up with the incredible party décor shown on influencers’ posts, and you don’t have to try. Elegance can be found in any space, so host within the realities of your home. “You are not meant to be entertaining at the level of someone with a million-dollar budget and a gigantic home. You get to entertain at exactly your level, whatever that is,” Post indicates. “All the little touches and the things you do to make people feel comfortable and welcome in your home are what make for a great host.”.

Bringing the wrong item can be an error on the part of the guest, but hosts should always make sure to minimize discomfort. “You want to take the etiquette high road and let it not be a problem. If [someone brings] an extra guest, swiftly enlist someone from your household or a trusted guest to help you zhuzh the arrangements in a discreet way so that the extra person does not feel like they were not meant to be there… [We have] the nearest-and-dearest to the host take smaller portions, so that everyone can have a decent portion.”.

Part of smartphone etiquette is letting others make their own choices. “You don’t overly control someone’s phone usage. Their rudeness will show on its own and will be noticed by more than just you… [Saying] ‘Could you make sure your phone is off, so you’re not tempted to use it throughout the evening?’ That is not a polite thing, even though it sounds gentle and so reasonable. That’s micromanagement.”.

Recent findings suggest that bringing a thoughtful gift is always appreciated, but truly engaging with the event is what really matters. “There is no burden for hosting you. You’ve been invited and should feel welcome and like you belong in this space. You are not there to repay the efforts of the host. We are greeting our host. We are engaging with the other people. We are helping ourselves to the refreshments that are offered. If there are games or entertainment, we’re participating in that. If there’s a theme, we’ve showed up in the theme. That’s really how we’re a good guest.”.

Sources indicate that always say goodbye. “At the end of the night, say thank you and goodbye and seek out the host, whether it’s a massive open house party or it’s a small dinner party to make that connection and express gratitude before we go.”.

Serving an item that a guest brought is at the host’s discretion. “A hostess gift is a hostess gift. It is not meant to be used that night with the people who brought it. It can be, but it does not have to be.”.

Whether you mail a card or not, make sure to share your appreciation with your host. “Thank-you notes are a wonderful idea and they allow you an extra level of expression, a little more thought. It doesn’t mean that a text message the next day would not also be appreciated. Any version of thanking your host after a party is a great version.”.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

This Piping Hot Zenith Collaboration Explains the Future of the Watch Market

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that zenith recently announced that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market.
  • Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Company, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November. The latest Zenith G.F.J., made in partnership with the Los Angeles-based independent watchmaker J.N. Shapiro, is a gorgeous timepiece that combines the former’s mechanical know-how with Shapiro’s meticulously handmade dials. Over four months before the watch was even unveiled to the public, Marietta shared that 20 of the 25 pieces produced had already been sold. Of all the releases from the major Swiss brands in 2026, none better represent the future of luxury watchmaking than this high-end, fussily made, independent-adjacent, sold-out-before-you-ever-heard-about-it G.F.J.

It has been revealed that zenith recently announced that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market. “All of us in our segment, which is described as mid-range, are going through a very difficult period,” Zenith CEO Benoit De Clerck told staff as he explained the restructuring, according to Le Temps. The brand has been shifting upmarket since last year, when it released a rainbow gem-set version of its flagship sport watch. The G.F.J. is the cornerstone of that new business. As the economy tilts even further in favor of the uber-rich, it’s also altering where the bulk of the profits come from for watchmakers. “Wealthy people are still wealthy, and even more wealthy,” Marietta said. “It’s easier [now] to sell high-end watches than watches for 3,000 to 5,000 Swiss francs.”.

That’s true. Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Company, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year. Not for the brand’s flagship Chronomaster, which remains firmly in the starter luxury watch zone at $12,300, but for the far more expensive G.F.J., which starts at $49,900. “The luxury direction is the game changer,” Monroy stated. Feldmar only received three G.F.J.s to allocate in 2026 and they were all quickly snapped up. There’s now a waitlist building at the retailer for the upscale model.

When it comes to the G.F.J., Zenith has acted like MacGyver, finding endless uses for its smash-hit model. First released in the spring of 2025, the watch received two very pretty, well-received sequels earlier this year. In March, I got to test out the new onyx-dial version for just a few hours before I had to send it along to Hollywood stylist Fabio Immediato, who promptly strapped it on Simu Liu’s wrist for the Oscars.

Over the summer, Zenith also introduced this double-signed program, which allows the brand to work with independent makers like J.N. Shapiro. Before this latest release, the Swiss brand linked up with Japan’s beloved Naoya Hida.

It has been revealed that that watch was a fascinating representation of the project—the spotlessly clean dial was straight out of the latter’s workshop. Zenith, a historic brand backed by LVMH, ceded control entirely to the small Japanese indie. It was a massive success. To allocate the pieces, Marietta said they narrowed the list to 10 clients, mainly from the Naoya Hida side, then sent an email that included the price tag of 60,000 Swiss francs but zero images of the watch. “They said yes right away, trusting us with the design,” Marietta said. “And that’s a great testimony of how the trust can be at that level when you buy a piece for [$75,000] without even seeing it, not even a picture.”.

In a recent development, in the topsy-turvy world of watches in 2026, it’s much sexier to be an independent brand than one in the stable of the world’s largest luxury conglomerate. Marietta calls the G.F.J. “an independent brand within our global lineup,” pointing to the high-level finishing and historic movement inside the piece—the type of nerdy details that appeal to the most seasoned collectors driving the industry. “The G.F.J. collection itself is bringing us fresh clients,” Marietta said. “It's attracting clients who did not really have Zenith on their radar. These guys were more A. Lange & Söhne clients or with independents.”.

In a recent development, zenith created irresistible bait for this newly introduced stripe of collectors. The new J.N. Shapiro-designed G.F.J. is absolutely gorgeous. The partners leverage the LA independent’s dedication to creating its dials by hand through a technique known as engine turning. I got to visit Shapiro’s workshop a few years ago and was charmed by the contrast of the brand’s cavernous industrial warehouse and the row of almost medieval-looking engine-turning machines lined up at the front of the room.

The dials of the latest collaborative watches were painstakingly made on those very machines—on which a single mistake means tossing the whole thing in the bin—and then shipped off to Switzerland, where Zenith watchmakers installed them into cases. There are three different patterns on the dial, including a basketweave at the center and Shapiro’s signature invention, the Infinity Weave, inside the subdial. Much like on the Naoya Hida version, the dial is all Shapiro. Marietta notes, however, that it already resembles the brick pattern seen on the original G.F.J., which is based on the exterior of Zenith’s manufacture in Le Locle.

Zenith plans to release two collaborative versions of the G.F.J. annually moving forward. According to Marietta, a couple of years down the road, the brand may allow their indie partners to go beyond the dial and play with the case and movement as well.

Sources indicate that with the G.F.J., Zenith has created something that is tailor-made for today’s collectors. Seven-figure pieces are right now booming at auction, and it would take Moses himself to part the money flooding into the market right now. These deep-pocketed collectors are most interested in watches from independent makers: Auction houses have sold more million-dollar F.P. Journe watches this year than they have from either Rolex or Patek Philippe. As collectors search for the next hot watchmaker, they’re finding exactly what they’re looking for in a 161-year-old Swiss luxury brand.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

In a recent development, combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Industry observers note that add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This year’s best documentaries spanned a wide range of subjects and themes, but every film on this list passes the same test: It asks hard questions and makes it impossible to look away.

In a recent development, that matters right now. The news comes at us in a relentless stream of stories about dehumanizing technology, unnecessary wars, and devastating climate collapse. It should rattle all of us. Instead, most days, we simply scroll past. These films force us to slow down, look closely, and listen to voices we may otherwise miss, like that of a young boy in West Texas who writes a play about Stalin, or Harlem Renaissance icons arguing over drinks in footage that sat untouched for 50 years.

The list is in no particular order.

It has been revealed that naza is one of this year’s most disturbing documentaries. In 80 minutes, set on Tel Aviv rooftops at night, with a city full of life gleaming in the background, we hear 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel—their faces and names protected by anonymity—describe the cold calculations made by themselves and others in Gaza following the October 7 attack. One soldier describes the AI tools he helped build, enabling the IDF to decide how targets are flagged, how much error is tolerated, and how many civilians—mostly women and children—it is acceptable to kill. The work is compared, more than once, to a video game.

Sources indicate that what makes the film essential viewing is its unflinching evidence of how institutional logic sanitizes mass casualties. Despite many insisting that the film is riddled with inaccuracies, it undoubtedly raises questions that demand full answers.

In You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder follows convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, en famille, in the weeks before she goes to prison, and he strays from every rule of documentary filmmaking. He seems to have iterated the form into a latest dimension—The Real Housewives of the penitentiary crossed with 60 Minutes—that is perhaps the perfect mirror to hold up to Holmes. He is also in the frame, and he’s steering hard.

Billy Evans, Holmes’s partner and the film’s undeniable villain, claims something so perfectly deranged in every scene that it plays as almost scripted. Holmes professes innocence throughout, even as her behavior argues otherwise; she controls every conversation, including the ones about her control. The film never lays out the case against her but really doesn’t need to. After almost three hours in her company, you feel as worked over as any of her scammed investors.

In 1972, William Greaves threw a party at Duke Ellington’s Harlem townhouse and invited every surviving contributor to the Harlem Renaissance he could find. Aaron Douglas. Arna Bontemps. Eubie Blake. James Van Der Zee. The list goes on. Many hadn’t seen each other in decades. Fifty years later, Greaves’s son David made this film with that footage.

Recent findings suggest that you can study the Harlem Renaissance in a classroom. You can read the material and revere the names. But nothing prepares you for the people, older then but still very much alive, in a living room arguing, interrupting, laughing at each other, still fighting over what it all meant. Nobody is a monument—that’s the film’s trick. It takes figures history had already embalmed and lets them be loud.

Recent findings suggest that john Wilson took a workshop on how to sell a Hallmark movie, then tried to use the formula to sell a documentary about concrete. That’s technically the premise of The History of Concrete, his first feature, and it’s as close as you can get to a walk through someone else’s brain.

For the first stretch, you don’t know where you’re going. Neither, it seems, does Wilson. Then the detours start to connect. Wilson pursues the people most others would avoid: strangers mid-ramble, mid-obsession, too odd to be invented. His unpretentious point of view is singular, and what he finds is universal. Also, it’s one of the funniest films you’ll watch this year—until, without warning, it breaks your heart.

When a Witness Recants is a detailed and harrowing account of how, in 1983, three Baltimore teenagers were convicted of murdering a 14-year-old classmate for his jacket and ended up serving 36 years for a crime they never committed. In fact, Alfred Chestnut, Ransom Watkins, and Andrew Stewart made history by spending a combined 108 years in prison—the longest for a wrongful conviction in the United States. The evidence that led to their eventual exoneration sat in a police file for all that time.

The film chronicles malfeasance at every level, including a detective coercing child witnesses, an obvious other suspect who was never pursued, and staggering misconduct by judges and prosecutors. It is impossible, as a viewer, not to be moved by the weight of the final act, when the men meet with the witness—then himself a teenager—whose false testimony hijacked their lives. Ron Bishop attempts to explain his side of the story (coercion and all), and the men politely listen. But what they really want is an apology. The exchange is stilted, unsatisfactory—and perhaps that is inevitable. What was done to these men was not the work of a single scared teenager, but of a system that failed them catastrophically. To capture the emotional magnitude of such injustice is a very tall task. The documentary succeeds by trying.

In a recent development, nuisance Bear follows polar bears living at the edge of a town in northern Canada, where tundra and parking lots collide. The question it asks is simple: Who is the nuisance here? Inuit elder Mike Tunalaaq Gibbons narrates, explaining how his people and the bears have been similarly disrupted—relocated and then barely tolerated within their newly introduced surroundings.

The film works most powerfully through sound. Helicopters thrum, ATVs whine, and under it all, the bears growl back. This is not a wildlife film in the usual sense. The bears are not observed in their habitat. They are watched at the fence line, where progress grinds against them.

Most nature documentaries take natural life and arrange it around a familiar narrative, finished with a neat ending. Nuisance Bear is shot like one but refuses to behave like one.

Before she was the woman who beat Donald Trump in court twice, E. Jean Carroll was Miss Cheerleader USA; a pioneering editor at Esquire, Playboy, and Outside; and, for 26 years, the advice columnist who helped Elle readers navigate life’s mess. Ivy Meeropol’s film covers all of it, and after witnessing Carroll spend decades telling women to toughen up and stand up for themselves, the through line is obvious. Soon, she was put in a position to practice what she preached.

Recent findings suggest that the trial footage is the draw, but her columns buoy the film. Meeropol shows how a persona built in print and on camera became the thing the defense used against her: She was too loud, too funny, too much for a victim. But Carroll refused to tone it down. Ask E. Jean is a conventional portrait but a compelling one, because the subject—now in her 80s—never flinches or asks to be liked.

Sources indicate that the Boys and the Bees is one of this year’s short-film triumphs. In it, we meet Eliza and Nehemiah Ray and their two young sons, Carver and Aaro, living on 12 acres in rural Georgia. We witness the parents’ patience and care for their boys, their bees, and the land that sustains them.

One moment captures the film’s beauty. Carver, the only one in the family yet to be stung by a bee, wants to know what his parents and brother have felt. Nehemiah looks him in the eye and tells him the truth: it’s going to hurt. Carver screams and cries, and his father stays close as it burns, pulling out the stinger. By the end, with his father beside him, Carver is proud of himself.

In a recent development, it’s every lesson at once. To tell the truth, even when it’s hard. To let yourself be pushed but also held. Few films this year say so much in so little time.

In a recent development, luis Valdez picked crops as a kid growing up in California. Then, in 1965, he founded El Teatro Campesino and staged plays on flatbed trucks for striking grape pickers, who agitated for the first union contracts for farmworkers. Zoot Suit, the play he wrote and directed about the 1943 Los Angeles riots, became the first Chicano production on Broadway, though the critics dismissed it. Valdez went on to make the Ritchie Valens biopic La Bamba, which became one of the biggest hits of 1987. This film tells that story in order, and the order is the argument. Each time Valdez faced rejection, he adapted—eventually landing himself on bigger stages. It is a standard talking-heads tribute, but the archival footage of performances alone is worth the watch.

It has been revealed that my last pick is the charming New York Times op-doc Stalin Boys, in which four West Texas middle schoolers write and perform a play about Stalin’s purges to compete in the Texas State History Fair. A middle school boy named Malachi is obsessed with one of the most ruthless dictators the world has ever known; this surely raises eyebrows at school. But his interest is rooted not in admiration but in a healthy curiosity about humanity’s rawest edges.

Industry observers note that at one point, Malachi describes Stalin’s father as a drunk who turned cruel. Then, quietly, he mentions his own father, also a drinker, whom he and his mother escaped when they came to Marathon, Texas.

Malachi’s fascination with such dark material is bound up with his own helplessness. Yet the film offers hope at a time when the AI-induced atrophy of young minds and the general outsourcing of curiosity looms so large. We get to smile when we see him practicing his Russian accent with YouTube videos. We see the little boy feel powerful donning a Soviet uniform with dangling medals. More adults, not just middle schoolers in a dwindling railroad town in the high desert of West Texas, should be asking questions like, “So, why’d he turn out like that?”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the recent buzz around peptides came to a head last month when U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. unveiled that six unregulated injectables, including the highly controversial “Wolverine stack” BPC-157 and TB-500, will now be available for broad use throughout the United States. Meanwhile, unsurprising to derms and estheticians everywhere, the rising tide of interest in peptides has spilled over into skincare, where the molecules have long served as an active ingredient.

“I’ve had a lot of patients come in since the HHS ruling,” notes Erik Peterson, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City, who likens the recent policy change to “opening the floodgates,” resulting in a surge of interest—particularly from patients who’ve come across claims of peptide-based skincare being like ‘botox in a bottle.’.

“It’s interesting how they are suddenly so popular, because peptides have been around for like 30 years in skincare,” says Malika Sloan, medical esthetician and founder of Sloan Studio in New York City. “They’ve been incorporated into cosmetic formulations for decades, with ingredients like matrixyl helping to popularize them in the early 2000s. What’s exciting now is how much more sophisticated the formulations have become.”.

If you’re curious about peptide-based skincare products—what they potentially can do, what they definitely cannot—and which products experts recommend for the best results, here’s everything you need to know.

Peptides, regardless of whether they’re injected via syringe or applied topically with a serum or cream, are short chains of amino acids that instruct your body to execute specific functions. Insulin, for example, is a peptide that helps the body regulate blood sugar, and it’s been in use since the 1920s. More recently, GLP-1 drugs (short for glucagon-like peptide-1) have been found to curb food cravings and slow stomach emptying, making them highly effective for weight loss. The list of uses for peptides is virtually endless, ranging from muscle growth and wound healing to balancing hormones and managing inflammation.

Sources indicate that in skincare, topical peptides work much the same way as their injectable counterparts, but on a more localized level, directing your skin to carry out specific functions, “the first of which tends to be increasing production of collagen and elastin, which are two of the major determinants of skin quality,” says Dr. Peterson. They’ve also been shown to help even out skin tone, repair the skin barrier, and reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles.

According to recent reports, the world of peptides is still a bit of a Wild West. A quick Google search for peptide skincare will yield dozens of results for unresearched compounds promising you flawless skin. And then, of course, there are the influencers. “You see all these kids on TikTok who are talking about their beauty routines, and they’re like 19 years old,” states Peterson. “It’s like, ‘Amazing, your skin obviously looks great, because you’re a child.’” In reality, the list of peptides that you can truly depend on to move the needle (without an actual needle) is surprisingly short, at least until more research is done.

“The two peptides that are out right now that have any sort of viable data on them are palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 and GHK-Cu,” states Peterson. Signaling peptides, as they’re called—such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, better known as matrixyl—have some of the strongest clinical and anecdotal evidence for stimulating collagen and reducing the appearance of wrinkles. Although, as Peterson points out, much of the scientific data has been industry funded, “so we always have to be a bit skeptical.”.

Carrier peptides—like GHK-Cu, a popular copper peptide—on the other hand, “have some good lab data, but very minimal human data,” Peterson indicates. Nonetheless, products containing GHK-Cu are widely heralded for their ability to repair damaged tissue, reduce inflammation, and stimulate production of collagen and elastin. “I find copper peptides particularly interesting because of the research surrounding tissue repair and collagen-related remodeling pathways,” says Sloan.

According to recent reports, as for acetyl hexapeptide-8, or argireline, as it’s more commonly known—aka “botox in a bottle”—don’t waste your money. “From a physiological perspective, it can’t possibly work,” states Peterson, who explains that the molecules of this particular peptide are simply too large to pass through the surface of the skin. He compares it to skincare products that contain collagen rather than spur the body to produce its own. “Collagen is a massive molecule,” he says. “It would be like putting cow’s milk on your face—it’s not going to do anything.” Sure enough, a 2023 study found the effects of topical argireline to be “not statistically significant.”.

According to recent reports, instead, for those looking for the most noticeable results, Sloan recommends seeking out products that combine proven peptides with complementary, similarly validated ingredients—like SkinCeuticals’ P-TIOX Anti-Wrinkle Peptide Cream. “I like that the cream also incorporates ceramides, niacinamide, and moisturizing ingredients, making it an interesting option for someone looking to address both hydration and visible signs of aging,” she states. Peterson’s pick, The Rich Cream from Augustinus Bader, flanks signaling peptides with hyaluronic acid and vitamin E to improve moisture retention and bolster the skin’s protective barrier.

Peptides are a relatively low-maintenance addition to most skin regimens. “One of the reasons I love incorporating peptides into at-home skincare is that they’re generally well tolerated and relatively easy to combine with other ingredients,” indicates Sloan, who notes that peptides can typically be used alongside other popular actives like vitamin C, niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, and retinoids. “I typically recommend incorporating a peptide serum after cleansing and before moisturizer,” she says.

Just keep in mind that peptides alone won’t take the place of a well-rounded skincare regimen. “The best, most robust data still comes from the tried-and-true favorites of all dermatologists—protecting your collagen with consistent sunscreen use, and the best signaling molecule of them all: topical retinoids,” Peterson says.

In a recent development, and, of course, don’t expect overnight results—despite what social media might have you believe. “Peptides are just signals for your skin, not magic in a bottle,” Peterson says. “The few studies that there are show at least three months of consistent usage before results are seen, so stick it out if you want to give it a real try.”.

Breaking: As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that senate Minority Leader Charles E.
  • As Democrats continue their victory lap after their major wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.
  • For Senate Democratic leader Charles E.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their major wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”.

“The most key lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he mentioned at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their intends could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer noted, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”.

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”.

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he stated Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the newly introduced session.”.

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

According to recent reports, the group isn’t alone in floating a latest approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Industry observers note that sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”.

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”.

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”.

Sources indicate that it would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Recent findings suggest that many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”.

Industry observers note that “For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he remarked, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”.

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the upcoming Congress, mentioned at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”.

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth mentioned in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”.

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”.

Recent findings suggest that but it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of Fresh Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he remarked.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

Recent findings suggest that “I wanted to live in a white cube, only to end up building a whole business around the interiors I grew up in,” claims Martina Mondadori, a Milanese tastemaker and the co-founder and editor in chief of Cabana. Mondadori’s home, dubbed Casa Cabana, is a true expression of that sensibility: a richly layered apartment designed by Renzo Mongiardino, the master of theatrical interiors and modern baroque, who was a close friend of her mother, its original owner.

In a recent development, mondadori carried that more-is-more, layered sensibility into both Cabana, her lifestyle magazine turned home brand, and the way she entertains. Her Milan Fashion Week luncheons, hosted at her family home, have become a social fixture for a stalwart collective of designers, artists, and friends of the brand—from ELLE editor-in-chief Nina Garcia and La DoubleJ designer J.J. Martin to architects Roberto Peregalli and Laura Sartori Rimini—who gather over fresh pasta, delicious antipasto, and mouthwatering desserts beneath a canopy of color and pattern.

Sources indicate that “Ambiance is not only décor; it’s how you entertain, how you bring your friends and family together, how you gather them around the table—the food, the scent, the music,” she says, noting that it can take more than two years for a house to truly feel like home. “Mongiardino was so good at [creating ambiance] because he knew how to make coziness happen.”.

For Mondadori, a beautiful table or a beautifully decorated space is only the beginning. She notes that any worthwhile gathering requires a “surgical” guest list layered with people from a “mishmash of different worlds,” plus tactile, personal touches like handmade place cards (often designed by her daughter, Cosima) and a guest book to capture the evening—her favorite hostess touch. Years later, its pages become a record of the people who have gathered around her table.

According to recent reports, you have to be surgical about it. Whatever the size of the party, you need at least one or two great conversation starters—people who can bring others together and spark interesting connections. I also love mixing crowds from different industries, which a city like Milan, Newly introduced York, or London allows. When I was growing up in Milan in the ’80s, the fashion crowd and old industrial Milan were separate. Now there’s a much bigger creative industry, along with interesting visitors from abroad. I love bringing those people together.

Recent findings suggest that we usually spend Christmas Eve and Christmas Day in the mountains with our extended family. We play board games, sit around the table, and exchange gifts—it’s all about creating a happy atmosphere. I ask my daughter to craft the place cards. When we moved here, she was 4, and so the first ones were all kind of scrabbled and very sweet. And now she’s very artistic, so they’re getting more creative and neat.

A guest book. Every hostess who loves entertaining loves to have a beautiful guest book where everyone can leave a little note.

According to recent reports, divinity candy is a classic Southern dessert. If you haven't heard of it yet, I promise you'll be coming back to this recipe over and over again after making it just once! It’s a simple confection made of sugar, eggs, and corn syrup that looks like clouds, with the crunch of meringue and the chew of a perfect marshmallow. It does require a candy thermometer and a bit of patience, but once you know what to look for, it’s extremely simple to make.

In the large bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment, combine the egg whites and salt.

According to recent reports, in a medium pot, combine the sugar, corn syrup, and water. Attach a candy thermometer to the pot before you go any further. Heat the mixture over medium-high heat, undisturbed, until the thermometer registers 250°, which should take about 10 minutes. When the thermometer registers 235°, start whipping egg whites on high speed until stiff peaks form, which should take another 2 to 3 minutes.

It has been revealed that with the mixer running on medium speed, carefully add sugar syrup to egg whites in a thin stream. Make sure to go slowly! The whole process should take about 1 to 2 minutes. Then beat in the vanilla extract.

Recent findings suggest that proceed to increase mixer speed to high and continue to whip until the mixture comes together and loses some of its gloss, which should take approximately 5 to 10 minutes. Let it all cool until the mixture is slightly thickened and holds its form when spooned onto parchment, another 1 to 2 minutes.

According to recent reports, grease 2 spoons with cooking spray, and working rapidly, spoon candy onto a parchment-lined baking sheet. Swirl it as desired to make the shapes you want! Immediately top the dessert with sprinkles. (The sprinkles won’t stick if you wait too long!).

Let the candy sit until it’s completely dry, just about 2 hours more. Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 1 week and enjoy!

This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Industry observers note that bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.).

Breaking: What the EU’s Blueprint to Abandon the Green Claims Directive Means for Fashion

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on November 4, the European Commission placed the proposed Green Claims Directive on a list of legislation it intends to withdraw within six months.
  • The November listing confirms an intention the Commission first signaled in June 2025, prompting the Council to cancel a planned final round of negotiations.
  • If withdrawn, the directive’s prescribed substantiation and pre-publication verification process would never take effect, sparing companies some upfront costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on November 4, the European Commission placed the proposed Green Claims Directive on a list of legislation it intends to withdraw within six months. The proposal would have set common rules for substantiating and independently verifying voluntary environmental claims. Its planned withdrawal comes just five weeks after separate anti-greenwashing rules began applying across the EU, leaving fashion brands with continued obligations and less direction on how claims should be proven.

The November listing confirms an intention the Commission first signaled in June 2025, prompting the Council to cancel a planned final round of negotiations. The proposal remains formally pending until the withdrawal process is completed, although its revival appears unlikely. The Commission indicates efforts to advance it during 2025 failed and that it is unlikely to secure sufficient support from member states within a reasonable timeframe.

If withdrawn, the directive’s prescribed substantiation and pre-publication verification process would never take effect, sparing companies some upfront costs. Existing obligations under the EU Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive, or EmpCo, and broader consumer law would remain, leaving companies to interpret the rules and carry the legal risk.

Recent findings suggest that empCo has already strengthened EU consumer law against greenwashing, including restrictions on unqualified claims such as “green” and “eco-friendly”, sustainability labels that lack a qualifying certification scheme or public authority behind them, and product claims of carbon neutrality based on offsetting. It also requires claims about future environmental performance to be supported by a detailed implementation plan with measurable targets and regular independent verification.

The Green Claims Directive would have gone further by prescribing how companies should substantiate explicit environmental claims — for example, that a garment has a lower carbon footprint or uses less water — and requiring independent verification before those claims reached consumers. Its withdrawal could leave brands with fewer mandatory steps but less certainty about the evidence regulators will expect.

According to recent reports, for fashion, the question of proof travels upstream. Consumer-facing claims often depend on data from textile mills, garment factories and raw-materials suppliers; as brands develop their own evidence requirements, manufacturers serving several customers could face a sprawling patchwork of reporting demands.

Withdrawing the directive would eliminate a prescribed substantiation and verification process, along with some of its upfront costs. Companies would still need to assess their claims and supporting evidence under EmpCo and existing consumer law, placing more of the judgment and legal risk inside the business, leading to uncertainty.

Sources indicate that that uncertainty is already being felt inside fashion companies. One sustainability executive at a fashion brand, speaking on background because they were not authorized to discuss the organization’s regulatory preparations, says the rapid succession of EU rules has left substantial room for interpretation, making compliance difficult even for companies acting in good faith.

Though brands would avoid some of the initial costs associated with the proposed verification regime, they will still need to identify potentially risky claims, assess whether the underlying evidence supports them and decide when further substantiation, qualification or other safeguards are necessary. That analysis will happen claim by claim, with national regulators and courts interpreting the common EU rules as cases emerge.

The attorneys say companies should hold evidence that directly relates to the claim, remains current and can be independently verified. EmpCo provides clearer boundaries around prohibited practices, but it does not supply the comprehensive methodology that the Green Claims Directive was intended to establish.

Sources indicate that that leaves room for differences among EU member states. EmpCo establishes a common EU legal baseline, and the attorneys expect national approaches to remain broadly similar. Member-state regulators and courts could still apply those rules differently to individual claims, particularly before further guidance and case law emerge.

The European Commission could reduce some of that uncertainty through guidance and coordination, but it cannot fully recreate the detailed, harmonized framework envisioned by the abandoned proposal, the attorneys add.

Consumer advocates are particularly concerned about the loss of pre-publication verification. EmpCo enables authorities to challenge prohibited or misleading claims after they enter the market. The Green Claims Directive would have required covered claims and labels to clear an independent check beforehand.

National enforcement authorities already face limited resources and an enormous volume of environmental marketing, say Blanca Morales, head of sustainable consumption and production at the European Consumer Organisation, known as BEUC, and Patrycja Gautier, its head of consumer rights and product safety.

In a recent development, assessing the evidence behind a claim can require technical expertise and lengthy investigation. In the meantime, the marketing remains visible. Claims can circulate for years before authorities intervene, Morales and Gautier say, by which point “the harm is already done”.

According to recent reports, the absence of a common methodology also makes comparison harder. Companies may use different calculations to describe the environmental footprint of clothing, leaving shoppers unable to assess products on equivalent terms. The problem is particularly acute in fashion, where retailers and platforms have introduced an array of proprietary sustainability scores, labels and filters, notes BEUC.

The planned withdrawal could therefore reduce certainty for companies as well as consumers. EmpCo prohibits generic environmental claims unless a organization can demonstrate recognized environmental performance and creates specific rules for labels, future targets and offset-based marketing. It provides less direction on the methodology companies should use to substantiate other explicit claims.

Industry observers note that the enforcement picture could still evolve. On November 11, the Commission separately proposed changes to the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation that would allow it to investigate major cross-border infringements directly and impose fines of up to 6% of a company’s worldwide annual turnover. The proposal could strengthen enforcement against EU-wide greenwashing, but it must still pass through the legislative process.

Large fashion companies are unlikely to dismantle their sustainability systems because one proposed directive disappears.

“Our approach to sustainability is grounded in long-term commitments, not individual regulatory requirements,” says Jeff Hogue, head of global sustainability at Gap Inc. The firm will continue complying with applicable rules and believes environmental claims should be “clear, credible and supported by evidence”, he adds. Gap also favors consistent standards across markets, which it says help companies communicate progress while maintaining consumer trust.

Recent findings suggest that those long-term programs still depend on information from suppliers. Brands will likely continue requesting data on materials, energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, driven by corporate sustainability strategies, investor expectations, public pressure and other regulatory mandates, says Dr. Sheng Lu, professor and director of graduate studies in fashion and apparel studies at the University of Delaware.

That dependence creates legal exposure across the supply chain. A brand can face scrutiny under consumer-protection and advertising laws if its environmental claim is misleading or inadequately substantiated, even when the underlying information came from a supplier, notes Meaghan Colligan Hembree of DLA Piper. An upstream supplier may separately face exposure over representation made to the brand and its contractual obligations. How that risk is allocated will depend on the facts and the agreements between the parties.

With the Green Claims Directive’s proposed verification system unlikely to take effect, contracts and internal governance could carry greater weight. Hembree expects brands to scrutinize what suppliers are asked to represent, the substantiation accompanying that information, their audit and verification rights, how environmental data is updated and who bears responsibility for inaccuracies.

“From a litigation standpoint, that paper trail can become critically important in understanding who knew what, what the ultimate claim was based on, and where the information may have broken down,” she states.

According to recent reports, those requirements could vary by buyer. Large fashion companies already use their commercial leverage to determine which certifications, calculations and disclosures suppliers must provide, Lu says. Manufacturers serving several customers may then have to satisfy multiple standards and reporting systems, adding to the cost of collecting and sharing data.

According to recent reports, the burden will be particularly difficult for smaller suppliers, brands and exporters to absorb. Smaller brands and exporters without dedicated European legal teams may struggle to adapt their claims and evidence across national markets. Suppliers face a different burden: meeting multiple buyers’ data requirements, often without the staff or systems to do so, Lu says.

In a recent development, regulatory uncertainty could also shape sourcing decisions. Lu expects fashion companies to consolidate their supplier bases as they seek manufacturers with the infrastructure, data and trust needed to support environmental claims. Strategic supplier relationships will become more valuable when brands need reliable information extending from raw materials through production.

The early evidence may appear in product descriptions and sourcing questionnaires rather than corporate targets. Lu will be watching whether brands replace broad sustainability language with narrower, measurable claims, alongside changes in the data they require suppliers to provide.

Recent findings suggest that fashion companies should not wait for enforcement actions to establish the boundaries, the Loyens & Loeff attorneys say. They recommend reviewing environmental and social claims, checking whether sustainability labels meet the rules already in force, aligning language across consumer communications and creating processes to document and regularly reassess the supporting evidence.

“The framework may still develop, but the compliance obligation is already there,” the attorneys say, “and so are the risks of regulatory scrutiny, sanctions and civil litigation.”.

In a recent development, I would not be able to live in a home that has been created and decorated by an architect, because I like having my mess and books around. You must not have too many rules.

Christmas is a wonderful tradition in our home. I made a cushion embroidered with “Noël”—it’s such a lovely word in French. Our family has come together every Christmas since I got married. And of course, we love presents, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, photographer Anna Watt spent her summers at her family’s home in Montauk growing up. She had just finished her freshman year of college in 2017 when she met Tommy Powell, a second-generation commercial fisherman, at the family-owned bar and restaurant, The Montauket. And what began as a summer fling on Long Island would eventually turn into a nearly decade-long love story. “Over the course of almost 10 years, we always found our way back to each other,” Anna claims.

Recent findings suggest that “I introduced myself, but that wasn’t the beginning of ‘us’ just yet,” Tommy recalls. “It took running into her a few more times before I finally convinced her to go on a date with me. Persistence is key!”.

“I remember going back to college that fall and telling a friend, ‘I have a feeling I’m going to marry the boy I met this summer,’” Anna says.

In a recent development, as a commercial fisherman, Tommy spends 10 days at sea followed by 10 days on land, a schedule that has shaped the couple’s relationship. Whenever he takes an extended break from fishing, the two make a point of traveling together. In October 2024, they planned a trip to France and Portugal, with surfing and some much-needed time together on the agenda. “When we landed in Paris, I asked what the blueprint was for the weekend, and Tommy rapidly replied with ‘We’re going on a boat tomorrow!’” Anna remembers. “For someone who is typically very go-with-the-flow, I knew what this meant!”.

Sources indicate that on October 27, 2024, Tommy proposed beneath the Eiffel Tower aboard a small boat on the Seine. (Anna jokes that they like to have all their relationship milestones happen on boats.) “I like to think Anna had no clue it was happening,” Tommy states. “But that wasn’t exactly the reality of the day. That morning, she thought we had no plans, and when I told her we were going on a boat, I think she immediately knew something was up. It was perfect, though—out on the water, with the Eiffel Tower lit up just after sunset.”.

It has been revealed that nearly two years later, on September 18, 2026, the couple exchanged vows aboard the Mariner III on the Hudson River in Fresh York City, with 85 of their closest friends and family in attendance. For Anna, who works as a photographer, the wedding was an opportunity to bring her deeply personal vision to life. “I have a very creative type B brain,” Anna says. “I had a very specific vision and designed every detail of the day, down to the silverware, so intentionally.”.

Event planner Alex Reiss helped translate Anna’s ideas into reality—including one rather ambitious undertaking. When Anna couldn’t find rental furniture she loved, she enlisted her friend Dewi, an interior designer in Bali, to help her custom-design and import all of the furniture for the boat. “It was such a fun project,” Anna indicates. “I learned so much, and it ended up being one of my favorite parts of the process!”.

Sources indicate that the bride’s fashion journey took an equally unexpected turn. “I actually had a completely custom wedding dress made and ready to go,” Anna explains. “But then I saw the Jacquemus spring 2026 runway images and did a complete 180.” After falling for one particular look, she began calling the Jacquemus boutique in SoHo weekly, hoping to track it down. “Finally, this past spring, a sales associate I had been messaging called me and stated they had received one,” Anna remembers. “I immediately ran to SoHo with my friends Chris and Hanna to try it on and, somehow, it fit perfectly. Not a single alteration was needed!” It went home with her that day.

A traditional veil didn’t feel quite right with the dress, so Anna commissioned a custom scrunchie to match its trim instead. She kept her jewelry equally understated. “I’ve always been pretty minimal when it comes to jewelry,” she notes. “So I wanted to keep everything really simple.” For her something borrowed, she wore a vintage Greek charm bracelet belonging to her mother, while her friend Sophie Thorner, founder of Vice Versa, created custom stud earrings to complement her engagement ring. Another friend, Erin Pollard of Underwater Weaving, made a basket to hold her ceremony flowers, as well as a miniature blue basket for her “something blue.” Her something old was the garter her mother had worn at her own wedding, and for her second look, Anna turned to Laura Tønder of Kettel Atelier, who created a one-of-a-kind dress entirely from vintage crochet and doilies.
